articles.title: Startup Spotlight: Porchlight uses AI to help foster human connection in senior care
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: When a new caregiver walks into an assisted living room for a shift, they usually hold a chart with a room number and a list of medical needs — and almost no background about the human being in the bed. They might be caring for a former machinist, a retired dancer, or a veteran, but in the rush of daily care, those life stories are often left behind.
Seattle-area software engineer Patrick Donahue wants to bridge that gap.

Donahue is the founder and sole builder of Porchlight , a newly launched life-story and reminiscence tool designed for assisted living and memory care communities. With the tap of a single button on a device, a resident hears a prompt, records their memories, and lets the platform automatically generate a concise “Know Your Resident” briefing for care staff, as well as a private audio feed for family members.
The goal is to give busy aides immediate context on a resident’s history, turning routine care into meaningful human connection.

The project stems from Donahue’s own history — both as a veteran backend developer who spent years scaling web platforms and as the son of medical professionals exposed to hospice care. Seeing how easily personal histories disappear without deliberate recording, he set out to build a tool that makes daily storytelling effortless for residents and care teams alike.
Donahue shared his inspiration, the realities of early-stage software development, and the power of asking the right questions is this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.
In 50 words or less, what’s your elevator pitch?

Porchlight is a life-story tool for assisted living and memory care. A resident taps one button, hears a question, and talks about their life. Porchlight turns the answers into a briefing so every caregiver knows the person in the room, and a private page where family can listen and reply.
What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The first shift. The aide walking into a room tonight often knows a room number and a care plan and nothing else. The resident might have been a machinist, a dancer, a veteran, and nobody has had time to find out.

It’s personal for me. Both of my parents worked in medicine, and hospice care was part of our family’s life. When my father died, I understood how much of a person’s story goes with them unless someone asks while there’s still time. I’ve also kept a journal my whole life, and I know what putting your life into words does for you. Porchlight is the tool I wish had existed.
What surprised you after talking to customers?

I don’t have paying customers yet, and I’ve had fewer conversations with activity directors than I’d like. The surprise in the ones I have had: the first question wasn’t about the technology. It was what does it cost, and who has time to set it up. That pushed me to make setup a printed QR card and nothing else, and to make it free while communities try it.
How has AI changed the way you build your company?

It changed what’s possible. Transcription can now handle older voices, and language models can turn an hour of rambling memories into a one-page briefing or a family highlight. Our whole vision is to use that to strengthen human connection, never to replace it. There are three ways it does that:

What we’re after is a better quality of life, more dignity, and a way for residents to pass their wisdom on to the people they love. The resident talks and real people listen. Nothing in it pretends to be a person.
On the build side, I’ve spent ten years as a software engineer helping startups scale. AI coding tools are the reason a bootstrapped company can build and run something this careful at this pace.
What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

People hear “AI for seniors” and picture a companion chatbot, or a product only for people who are losing their memory. It’s neither. Reminiscence, meaning simply inviting someone to talk about their own life, is one of the oldest and most loved practices in eldercare, and it works for anyone with a life behind them. Porchlight makes it possible to do every day and keep what gets said. It isn’t a medical or therapy product, and I don’t claim it is.
What was the toughest decision you made in the past year?

Pulling claims off my own website. When I checked the marketing against the code, some of it described features that were planned, not built. Cutting that felt like making the product look smaller right when I needed it to look bigger. But I’m asking communities to trust me with their residents’ stories, so the copy has to match what the software actually does.
What’s one piece of advice for other entrepreneurs?
Make sure what you say matches what you’ve built. It’s tempting to describe the version in your head. Early on, trust is most of what you have to sell, and it’s easy to spend it without noticing.

A new aide walks into a room on their first day, asks a resident about the dance where he met his wife, and watches him light up. And the community pays for Porchlight because that moment is worth it to them.

articles.title: Tech Moves: Amazon GM departs for Scala; Flyhomes appoints 3 leaders; Heinz Marketing names COO
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Leadership changes at Bellevue, Wash.-based companies are dominating the news in this week’s Tech Moves, plus some notable items in neighboring Redmond.

— Former Amazon leader Asic Demberel is now chief technology officer for Scala , a Bellevue-based startup offering an AI operating system for contact centers and customer operations. Demberel was with Amazon for 15 years, first working on fraud technology for AWS and leaving the company as general manager and engineering leader for Amazon Pharmacy Kiosks.

“You don’t walk away from 15 years at Amazon for an incremental challenge. It takes an exceptionally complex problem and an opportunity so massive that you simply can’t look away,” Demberel said of his decision to leave.
Scala was founded by Smartsheet CEO Rajeev Singh and former Accolade executive Ardie Sameti. It raised an $8.5 million seed round in February.
— Flyhomes , a Bellevue-based company providing financial tools for home buying and selling, has named three leadership hires:

— Heinz Marketing , a Redmond, Wash.-based B2B marketing and consulting firm, is shaking up its leadership. The company has named Jenn Steele as its chief operating officer and president, while Matt Heinz , who started the business 18 years ago, is moving from president to CEO.

Steele joins Heinz Marketing from Seattle’s SoundGTM, which she co-founded and led. She has held executive roles at numerous Seattle-area companies including CEO of Kissmetrics and top marketing and revenue positions elsewhere.
Maria Geokezas is retiring as COO after nearly 17 years with the firm. The company credits her leadership with shaping the organization and said “the whole team is deeply grateful and will miss her.”
— Ludovic Fourrage announced that he is co-founder and chief AI officer for Untamed Intelligence , a Bellevue startup launched in May.

“Untamed Intelligence is an innovation studio dedicated to advancing human possibility. We begin by asking what human beings need to flourish and then explore how technology and learning science might help us get there,” the company said on LinkedIn.

Fourrage was previously senior program officer for the Gates Foundation. Before that, he was with Microsoft for more than 13 years, working in certification and learning leadership roles. Fourrage is also the founder of Nucamp Coding Bootcamp, serving as board chairman of the company.

The startup’s other co-founders are CEO Paul LeBlanc and Chief Product Officer Rachel Koblic . LeBlanc was president of Southern New Hampshire University for 21 years until 2024. Koblic has her own learning-focused consultancy and was chief learning officer for Matter and Space.
— LogicGate , a Chicago company offering a no-code governance, risk and compliance platform, has named two Bellevue-based leaders:

— The Technology Alliance has appointed Matt Medlin , a longtime CPA with a focus on venture-backed companies, chair of its board of directors. Two current board members have taken new roles, with Helion’s Jessie Thomas becoming vice chair and EY’s Alissa Garner Byersdorfer serving as treasurer.
The UW Climate Risk Lab has named two new members to its leadership council:
— Seattle-based Nimbus Aerospace , which recently completed a test flight of its quarter-scale prototype, has added two advisory board members:
— Evergreen Goodwill has promoted Derieontay Sparks to chief revenue officer, overseeing operations that support the nonprofit’s tuition-free education and workforce development programs.

— And in case you missed it, two top Microsoft executives shared this week that they’re leaving the Redmond tech giant: Peter Lee, the former head of Microsoft Research, and Ryan Roslansky, Microsoft executive vice president overseeing both LinkedIn and Microsoft Office. See the whole story here .

articles.title: Longtime Microsoft research leader Peter Lee and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky to depart
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Two top Microsoft executives announced this week that they’re leaving the Redmond, Wash., tech giant:
— Peter Lee , the former head of Microsoft Research and most recently president of Microsoft Science, is resigning after more than 16 years.

“As for what I’ll be doing next, what I can say at this point is that it is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to join an elite team, fulfilling a dream I’ve had since childhood. It’s a major detour from what I’ve been doing over the past 2+ decades,” Lee said on LinkedIn .
At the same time, he said he would continue working with healthcare organizations including the Mayo Clinic, Kaiser Permanente Bernard J. Tyson School of Medicine and Seattle Children’s.

Before joining Microsoft, Lee spent 22 years at Carnegie Mellon University, where he served as head of its Computer Science Department. He was named one of Time magazine’s 100 most influential people in health and life sciences in 2024.
As a hobby, Lee enjoys converting classic cars into electric vehicles, including a replica 1955 Porsche 550 Spyder and a 1968 Ford Mustang GT Fastback.

— Ryan Roslansky is leaving Microsoft after nearly 18 years with LinkedIn and Microsoft. Last year, he was promoted from CEO of LinkedIn to Microsoft executive vice president overseeing both LinkedIn and Microsoft Office. In April, the company named Daniel Shapero the new LinkedIn CEO.

Roslansky thanked CEO Satya Nadella, noting that when Microsoft acquired LinkedIn a decade ago, “you gave us room to build, and then trusted many of us with a lot more. I’ve learned more from you than I can fit in an email, and I’m grateful for the friendship that came with it.”

Nadella in turn praised Roslansky, saying on the company blog, “I’ve always appreciated his clarity of thinking and I’m deeply grateful for everything Ryan has built, for the leaders and teams he has developed, and for his friendship and counsel.”

Roslansky joined LinkedIn in 2009 as chief product officer and became CEO in 2020. To continue in his role as Microsoft EVP would require relocating his family from the San Francisco Bay Area to the company’s Redmond headquarters.
“But my life and my family’s life are here in the Bay Area,” he said, adding, “The work now goes to leaders who are set up to take it further. I can’t wait to see what they do with it.”
Roslansky will leave the company at the end of the year.

articles.title: New JPMorganChase Seattle tech leader: How AI is changing what the bank looks for in engineers
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Ture Armas has been encouraging JPMorganChase engineers, from Seattle to India, to rethink their approach to the job as AI changes how software gets built.

Armas, the new leader of the bank’s Seattle Tech Center, said in an interview that engineers will need to work more closely with the business, model its problems and communicate clearly, rather than waiting for a business analyst to hand them fully written requirements.
“Things that we in the past referred to as soft skills, they are now the hard skills,” Armas said, explaining that it’s changing how the bank hires. “You do need to interview for that.”

Lori Beer, JPMorganChase’s global chief information officer, named Armas to the Seattle role in July. He succeeded Mamtha Banerjee, who left the bank in March. Armas also continues in his day job as CTO and head of Commercial Bank Lending Technology.

How the job is changing: In his view, the traditional handoff from a business analyst, with wireframes and acceptance tests spelled out, is giving way to spec-driven development, in which engineers write the specifications that AI coding tools work from.

That puts a premium on skills such as modeling the business domain and working directly with business teams, much like the forward-deployed engineers that have become common in the AI industry. “We are moving towards that,” he said.
He gave the same advice to his teams in India on a recent visit, telling them to get embedded in the business and “fall in love with the business problem.”
Most developers at the Seattle center use GitHub Copilot, Armas said, while Anthropic’s Claude Code is in use on smaller teams.

On the bank’s July 14 earnings call , CEO Jamie Dimon said JPMorganChase has almost 1,000 AI use cases, about 50 of them significant, in areas including risk, fraud, marketing and document reading. He said the bank has “had discrete areas where we did reduce jobs by 30% or 40%,” and that “most of those people were offered jobs elsewhere.”
“We are preparing to make sure we can retrain our people,” Dimon said, predicting the change will be faster and more dramatic than past waves of automation.

A bigger footprint: The Seattle Tech Center has more than 400 people and about 50 open positions, mostly in AI, cloud and cybersecurity, said Kristine Baker , a JPMorganChase vice president who manages the Seattle Tech Center.

The team finished moving this summer into expanded space in the downtown Seattle skyscraper now called the JPMorganChase Center , formerly the Russell Investments Center. The bank occupies five floors in the building. Tech fills all of the 14th floor, the largest, with more technologists on two other floors.
The move brings the tech center back to where it started.

JPMorganChase opened the Seattle center in 2018 on a single floor of what was then the Russell Investments Center, led by Todd Hrycenko, a security executive who joined the bank from Salesforce. A year later, with about 100 people, it signed a lease at 1201 Third Ave., the former Washington Mutual Tower across the street.
The center grew to more than 320 people by 2023 under Rao Lakkakula, and to 380 by early 2025, when Banerjee took over after Lakkakula left for Microsoft.

Site leadership: Armas said he spends about 95% of his time on his lending technology job, and he credited Baker with running the tech center day to day. The lead role rotates among senior executives, and Baker has provided continuity through the changes in leadership.
“She shepherds each one of us along,” Armas said.

Baker joined JPMorganChase in 2023 from Amazon Web Services, where she led a program to build AWS teams at new U.S. locations, after 14 years at Western Washington University. She also works with the bank’s global program of about two dozen tech centers.

Armas, whose first name is pronounced too-RAY , grew up in British Columbia and studied computer science at the University of British Columbia. He worked in New York for about 18 years before moving to Seattle in 2016 to lead technology for the bank’s commercial real estate lending business, which has deep roots in Washington Mutual’s Seattle operations.

Seattle’s talent pool: Armas cited Seattle’s depth of talent in AI, cloud and cybersecurity engineering — noting, for example, that vets from Amazon and other local tech companies have moved into senior technology roles at the bank.

Beer, the bank’s CIO, said in a July interview that Seattle is one of the key hubs for a new AI software infrastructure team to help JPMC manage AI workloads across its own data centers and outside cloud providers, with the goals of controlling costs and avoiding lock-in to any one AI vendor.
The competition for engineers has eased since the hiring rush of the pandemic years. The bank is now getting “lots of responses to every position,” Armas said.

Asked about Seattle’s JumpStart payroll tax, which other business leaders have said discourages hiring in the city, Armas said there are no plans to change course from where the bank is now, in downtown Seattle.

Inside the office: The new tech floor in the JPMorganChase Center has become a draw for the rest of the bank. Armas said bankers regularly come up to the 14th floor, and when he asked some of them why, they told him the breakout room is the best in the building.

Desks on the floor aren’t assigned. They’re grouped into “neighborhoods” by line of business, including one for the bank’s AI and data organization, with lockers for personal belongings. Small rooms with doors line the floor for private calls, white noise keeps the open areas quiet, and windows look out over the city. There’s a prayer room and a mother’s room.
A game room with a ping-pong table sits behind an easy-to-miss door. Some employees have used it for DJ sessions, strobe lights included.

What’s next: The site lead role typically rotates every couple of years. Armas, who has been part of the conversations about a Seattle tech center since he arrived in 2016, said his goal over his tenure is to connect the center’s engineers with teams across the bank and the business problems the bank needs to solve.

articles.title: Kindle gets a clicker: Amazon unveils $35 page-turning remote and refreshes its e-reader lineup
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Amazon’s Kindle is joining the ranks of TVs and garage doors.

The company on Thursday unveiled the Kindle Click , a $34.99 Bluetooth remote control that lets readers prop up their e-readers and turn pages without holding or reaching for them. It’s the first official Kindle remote, debuting alongside a redesigned lineup of Kindle e-readers .

Amazon says it’s meant for reading under the covers, on a treadmill, or on an airplane tray table. It’s available for preorder and ships Oct. 28. It recharges over USB-C, includes side buttons for adjusting brightness, and works with Kindles released in 2024 or later.

The company cited BookTok as an inspiration, Bloomberg reported , a reference to the community of readers on TikTok who post book recommendations, reviews and their reading setups. Kindle fans there have been showing off third-party clickers for years.

Amazon is also bringing back physical page-turn buttons, which disappeared when the company discontinued the Kindle Oasis in 2024. This time they come in a separate $79.99 magnetic cover , which works only with the new Signature Edition versions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft.

The new Kindles have screens that sit flush with the edges, colors that wrap around to the front, and optional aluminum housings. They also have user-replaceable batteries to comply with European Union rules , Amazon told The Verge .

The base Kindle starts at $149.99, or $189.99 in aluminum . The Paperwhite starts at $199.99 and the Colorsoft at $289.99, with Signature Editions at $249.99 and $319.99 . Those prices match what Amazon has charged since August, when it raised Kindle prices by $40 to $50 , citing memory and storage costs. The base Kindle is available now. The Paperwhite and Colorsoft ship Oct. 28.

Amazon doesn’t disclose financial results or unit sales for its devices, but Kindle device sales hit their highest point in more than a decade last year, with three straight years of double-digit growth, Kevin Keith, Amazon VP of devices, said at a media preview, according to Bloomberg .

Chris Green, Amazon VP of industrial design, also told Bloomberg where he’d like to take the design next: “At some point we will get to something more like a credit card that’s all display that you’ll be able to flex with your hand for a page turn.”

articles.title: Starcloud’s AI computing payload will get a ride to lunar orbit on Firefly’s space vehicle
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: Redmond, Wash.-based Starcloud has signed up to send its artificial intelligence data-processing hardware into lunar orbit on a Firefly Aerospace spacecraft.

Starcloud’s payload, known as SC-1L, will fly on Firefly’s Elytra orbital vehicle during a NASA-supported mission that’s scheduled for launch no earlier than 2028. The mission will demonstrate technologies that Starcloud plans to use on AI data centers in Earth orbit — and around the moon as well.
“Space is the future of data centers, and the moon is the next frontier for that vision,” Ezra Feilden, Starcloud’s co-founder and chief technology officer, said today in a news release .

Starcloud made its mark in Earth orbit last year with Starcloud-1, a satellite equipped with an Nvidia H100 chip. Starcloud-1 successfully trained a large language model called NanoGPT, marking a first for orbital computing. “We successfully validated our ability to run and train AI models on enterprise-grade GPUs in low Earth orbit, and now we’re taking this proven technology to lunar orbit,” Feilden said.

Starcloud’s SC-1L payload will be integrated aboard the Elytra vehicle for a mission aimed at delivering Firefly’s Blue Ghost lander to a lunar region known as the Gruithuisen Domes . After the lander separates from Elytra and descends to the surface, the orbiting vehicle will serve as a data relay for Blue Ghost.

The data-processing demonstration begins when the Blue Ghost mission ends. SC-1L will ingest data from Elytra’s onboard Solux vision system , execute high-performance AI computing in orbit and transmit the processed data back to Earth.

The Solux system is designed to serve as an autonomous navigation and tracking tool in space environments where global positioning systems are otherwise unavailable. Firefly expects the Elytra orbiter to operate in lunar orbit for at least five years.

“We’re proud to collaborate with innovative customers like Starcloud and collectively take another step toward establishing the infrastructure that will power a permanent human and robotic presence at the moon,” said Ray Allensworth, Firefly’s vice president of spacecraft.

Elytra will also use high-resolution telescopes and Firefly’s Ocula moon imaging service for surface mapping, mineral detection and reconnaissance. Firefly recently announced a collaboration with Nvidia to process the data for Ocula using Nvidia’s Jetson module.

In August, Starcloud reported raising $250 million in funding to support the creation of a constellation of AI data-center satellites in low Earth orbit, powered by Nvidia’s Space-1 Vera Rubin Module. Starcloud has filed an application with the Federal Communications Commission to operate as many as 88,000 satellites as orbital data centers.

articles.title: Lake Hills Bus Trip
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: Today I’m taking you on my monthly bus trip to Lake Hills. I went on Saturday, September 26.

I feel so lucky riding Link across the late. No more express buses with congestion and turns and stoplights. Mt Rainier was visible, and a row of clouds looking like they’re sitting on an air shelf. Westbound cars were stuck in congestion from Mercer Island to Eastgate.
The transfer walk at South Bellevue station was 1:13 minutes. I was probably walking slowly.

Since I had a 20 minute wait for the bus, I did what I’ve never done and entered the P&R. I went to the top level and saw the view of the Slough, and counted the cars. There were around 225 cars. Level 3 goes to the station, but the most cars were on level 4. A guy on the top level was filming a video in front of his car.

The 226 is a U-shaped route on mostly Eastgate Way/SE 24th Street, 164th, and Bel-Red Road/NE 24th Street. My destination was right at the bottom of the U. I usually ride only the southern half, but today after my visit I rode the northern half to describe the rest of the route and clear up some misperceptions.

The threshold for a cost-effective bus route is 10 passengers per hour. The 226 got 11 in 22 minutes. So multiplying that by 3 gives 33 passengers per hour. People are riding it in the single-family neighborhoods, as I would if I lived there. Ridership was lighter today than other days.

On 164th it stops every two blocks, except between NE 6th and NE 16th (Northup) where it’s nonstop. This is the part that used to detour further east to the neighborhood I grew up in. So when it was rerouted to stay on 164th, no bus stops were added in the gap. South of NE 6th is all single family, and there’s a concentration of adult family homes. North of NE 6th are a few apartment buildings.

Interlake High School is at 164th & NE 24th. Weekday afternoons a dozen people would get on. Some of them got off if the detour further east that no longer exists. I don’t know what they do now. There’s no fixed-route service east of 164th any more; instead there’s a Metro Flex zone. I’m glad there was a fixed route when I lived there. But at the same time, the detour somehow added ten minutes to the trip. I hated it before it was extended to South Bellevue station and I had to ride it from Bellevue TC to Main Street and it took a whole 40 minutes.

Going from Main Street to 130th took around 15 minutes today. The time before it on a weekday it took more than 20 minutes. It’s a longish depressing walk from there to BelRed station (what CityNerd called “old Bellevue”),. So for me it’s not a compelling transfer westbound, and not at all eastbound where there’s no bench or shelter at the bus stop.

The 226 runs every 20 minutes peak hours, 30 minutes off peak, and 60 minutes evenings. Evenings starts at 4pm on weekends. I try to avoid it during that time, but since I’m more of a night owl than an early bird, sometimes I have to ride it then. This time I was ready to go but I would just miss it, so I waited 45 minutes at the home and then went out for it.

At 116th & NE 12th the 250 joins the route for 15-minute combined service the rest of the way. Overlake Hospital has two stops. Kaiser Permanente has one stop. A third stop is on the side of the library.

articles.title: This year’s Capitol Hill Christmas Dive Bar will temporarily take over storied nightclub space
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: It is October 1st so it is time to start thinking about… Christmas.
A storied Pike/Pine nightclub will be temporarily revived for the holiday season as this year’s edition of the Capitol Hill Christmas Dive Bar has found a new home.

Joey Burgess says the 2026 edition of the popular seasonal pop-up bar will make its home in the space previously home to Havana . While the longtime owner of Pike/Pine bars, clubs, and retail venues didn’t rule anything out, it is unlikely that the Christmas Dive Bar’s appearance has much to do with the old Havana’s future. Still, the planned pop-up will bring seasonal energy and festive crowds to the block at 10th and Pike through the holidays.
CHS reported here this summer as designer and musician Quentin Ertel announced he was closing Havana after 20 years of Pike/Pine nightlife.

Burgess and husband Murf Hall , meanwhile, have been busy downsizing their Pike/Pine business family after selling off their core neighborhood nightlife holding, Queer/Bar , to the ownership at The Cuff .

As for the Dive Bar, Burgess and Hall have turned the pop-up into a holiday tradition and a business opportunity strong enough to continue for their bottom line and the end of year finances of staff. Last year , Santa, snowflake, and Christmas lights took over the Queer/Bar space through December. The Christmas Dive Bar is usually lined up for a Thanksgiving-approximate debut.

The long-term future of the old Havana remains up in the air as does another key space in the the Hunters Capital- owned building. CHS reported here on the planned closure of the Capitol Hill Glossier as part of a worldwide pullback in the company’s retail ambitions. The store is set to be shuttered permanently in January. Meanwhile, neighboring Poquitos has new ownership .
The Christmas Dive Bar will return this year at 1010 E Pike. Follow @christmasdivebar for updates.

articles.title: Audits find Seattle Police tapping SDOT feeds sent by mistake — and private cameras on Capitol Hill
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Two newly released reports reveal that Seattle’s expanding camera network has outpaced city safeguards, sweeping up sensitive traffic feeds by mistake and pulling in private security cameras — including feeds on Capitol Hill — without clear rules.

Both audits were conducted under the Seattle Municipal Code which requires independent oversight offices to annually examine the Seattle Police Department and city’s approved surveillance tools for privacy risks, civil liberties impacts, and legal compliance.

The review by the Office of Inspector General warned that police and city leaders failed to set basic standards before connecting private business and property feeds into the Seattle Police Department’s Real Time Crime Center . Unlike city cameras, which use digital masking to black out apartment and hotel windows, the department cannot easily control third-party devices. If a business owner angles a camera into non-public spaces or archives video for months, police have no formal process to catch or correct the issue.

While the pilot has launched in downtown, Aurora, and the International District, investigators say the SPD plan to link private feeds citywide has been moving forward without adequate safeguards and has already integrated two private camera locations in Capitol Hill within SPD’s East Precinct without specific geographic limits.

OIG investigators concluded that the city’s approved surveillance impact reports left the rules for private cameras largely undefined, neither expressly permitting nor prohibiting expansion across the entire city. Although Mayor Katie Wilson paused adding city-owned cameras to new neighborhoods including the Central District and Capitol Hill , she did not state limits on private systems.

In August, police confirmed to auditors that they intend to accept integrations from any volunteering business across Seattle, and mapping revealed that the department had already activated two Capitol Hill private camera sites beginning in 2025.
The report did not disclose specific business names or street addresses for the two Capitol Hill sites, showing only their general orange placement pins on the department’s central integration map.

In March , CHS reported on a single security camera perched atop the Community Roots Housing mixed-use 12th Ave Arts development and focused on the street just across from the East Precinct headquarters at 12th and Pine. CHS asked a SPD spokesperson how the camera above 12th Ave was being used. “Security,” was the reply.

Meanwhile, a report by the City Auditor found that the Seattle Department of Transportation accidentally handed police access to technical roadway detection cameras that were not supposed to be shared. Unlike public traffic feeds visible on city transit maps, officials said these non-public cameras were sent to SPD on an integration list by error. SDOT is now attempting to revoke police access to those internal streams.

The findings come amid ongoing tensions over surveillance reach. The auditor cautioned that SDOT’s traffic camera decisions could carry unintended civil liberties consequences when linked to law enforcement. Police agreed to establish clear guidelines for private cameras by March 2027 and limit review to public spaces.

articles.title: Ambitious Capitol Hill hotel and restaurant project The Baillie is holding an estate sale
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The guys creating The Baillie boutique hotel and restaurant project on Capitol Hill’s Millionaire’s Row are holding an estate sale this weekend to clear out decades of furniture, knickknacks, art, and ephemera from the old mansion’s decades as a bed and breakfast.
Join us Sunday, October 4, 11-4pm at @thebaillieseattle as we open the doors for a one-day estate sale.

The new 14th Ave E project began with the $4.9 million acquisition of the Shafer Baillie Mansion and has been undergoing review with the city’s Seattle Department of Construction & Inspections since last fall. But first they need to clear out some space and find new homes for a few treasures.

articles.title: Seattle Permit Fees Get Another Hike Amid Development Slump
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Fees for building and land use permits in Seattle are set to see double-digit increases for the second year in a row, as the city grapples with lower permit volumes amid a bleak development environment. The 10.7% bump in Mayor Katie Wilson's proposed budget for the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections (SDCI) comes on top of an 18% increase just last year, adding costs to development right at a time when city leaders are hoping to spur construction.

With 91% of SDCI's budget coming from permit fees, the hike is a budget reality needed to maintain core staff, even as the department prepares to cut 34 fee-funded positions – including seven layoffs. But those added fees simply pile costs onto a dwindling constellation of projects that are able to move forward right now in the face of higher interest rates, increased construction costs, and an uncertain economic climate.

"These additional revenues help improve cost recovery, reduce the need for further staff reductions, and slow the use of fund balance while we continue to adjust to changing development activity," SDCI Finance Director Shane Muchow told city councilmembers Tuesday in breaking down the proposed budget.

SDCI expects Seattle to wrap up 2026 with 60% fewer applications for master-use permits (MUPs) than it saw in 2019, lower even than the depths of the Great Recession in 2010. Construction permit volumes are only expected to be 15% lower, but those permits have taken a dramatic shift toward smaller projects, a fact that impacts the amount of revenue that SDCI receives from them. All of these figures are spelling out a gloomy picture of the future of development activity in Seattle.

"That is very concerning to us in the department, when we see the scope and the valuation of the projects do not meet what they were in the the boom years, and the types of projects are smaller, less complex," Samuel Steele, SDCI's interim director, said.

Wilson put Steele in charge of the city's permitting department early this year after a prior string of temporary leaders for SDCI under former Mayor Bruce Harrell. Nathan Torgelson had led the department for nine years but left his post last March after Harrell requested his resignation . Steele previously led SDCI's construction inspection division.
Council land use committee chair Eddie Lin shared Steele's worries about the current development environment and what it portends for Seattle's housing goals.

"It's pretty alarming and concerning on many different levels," Lin said of the permit trends and the transition away from higher-value projects. Lin has been trying to advance the city toward its next major zoning update, delayed by legal challenges , but those upzones aren't likely to do the city much good if the economic climate – and Seattle's costly permit framework – mean projects aren't happening.

When these fee hikes are implemented, plan review and permit fees on a hypothetical 230-unit apartment building will have jumped from $274,486 in 2025 to $347,935 in 2027, a 26% increase. Costs to permit a four-unit townhouse development in Seattle will have jumped from $12,214 to $15,953 in just two years.

While those charges are far from the priciest line item on a developer's balance sheet, it's one more cost that could push a project on the edge of financial viability away from actually getting built.

The hope is that by raising fees, SDCI can stave off further erosion of its cash reserves long enough to make it to the next major uptick in the development cycle. Those reserves have taken significant hits in recent years. By the end of the year, the department expects to have fully exhausted the reserve devoted to maintaining core building and land use staff.

"We were generally between $80 million to $100 million through 2023, but since then we've gone down those balances significantly as permit revenues have declined," Muchow said. "By the end of 2026, we're projecting an overall fund balance of roughly $30 million dollars. The fee increases proposed for 2027, along with the expenditure reductions we discussed earlier, are expected to stabilize the fund balance and slow further erosion."

A jolt to the development pipeline could come as early as next year, with a proposal to temporarily reduce the hefty Mandatory Housing Affordability (MHA) fees , which are charged to builders in Seattle's densest zones to fund the City's affordable housing trust fund. The impact of the proposal could be limited, given its emphasis on reviving stalled projects that have already had their permits vested via an 80% discount on MHA fees, while new projects would only qualify for a 60% discount and need to break ground within two years of passage to claim the discount.

Meanwhile, around a half dozen neighborhoods mostly in the South End would be excluded from the program unless projects clear the additional hurdle of keeping ownership in the hands of a "legacy homeowner."

The Seattle Housing Roundtable , which represents around 30 developers and advocated for the fee reduction, has tallied more than 30 vested projects that they say would likely break ground with the 80% MHA break, leading to 6,000 new homes or more. The permit fees those projects would bring would be a nice bump for SDCI, but not enough to fix the department's long-term financial trajectory. The outlook for the next wave of projects looking to take advantage of the 60% discount is less certain, in part because the financial incentive is smaller.

MHA fees are a magnitude larger in scale that SDCI's permit fees. For example, on a hypothetical 230-unit apartment building, MHA fees may be $3 million or more, roughly 10 times greater than permit fees. Even after the proposed MHA break goes through, they would still exceed permit fees several times over.

Longer term reforms for Seattle's byzantine land use approval process could come about as a result of a new executive order that Wilson issued in August, which created a housing production task force charged with "developing and advancing policies and actions that accelerate housing production." In advance of that group's reports, due next year, Wilson has also set up an internal working group that is attempting to break down some of the siloes between different departments that all issue building permits.

"The Mayor's Office is leading a[n] interdepartmental team to really focus on some of these things. They have all the big departments involved: SDCI, of course, Department of Transportation, City Light, Public Utilities, the fire department, and one of the goals of this is to create end-to-end visibility," City Budget Director Aly Pennucci said Tuesday.

Even if reforms within SDCI are able to reduce costs for developers, the costs imposed by other regulations outside the department are significant as well, with rising utility costs coming under greater scrutiny . Wilson's budget for SDOT also includes increased fees for street use permits, with a 30% hike on deck for permit issuance, renewal, and modification.

"This was surprising to me to learn that currently, applicants need 30-plus permits from eight different departments to build housing in the city," Pennucci said. "So, that is one of the areas that are really being looked at, including really focusing on streamlining the speed of right-of-way and utility permitting, as those are kind of the longest duration [permits]."

While those reforms may ultimately bear fruit down the line, they aren't much help right now, and in the meantime the burden of keeping the city's permit infrastructure solvent will keep falling on exactly the type of projects that Seattle needs more of and is looking to boost.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Kirkland Must Raise its Wage Floor for Essential Workers
articles.author: Lam Nguyen Ho
paras: Everywhere in King County, tens of thousands earn poverty-level wages in stores, restaurants, hotels, healthcare facilities, and as janitors, landscapers, and more. But those in King County’s Eastside cities earn even less. On October 6, Kirkland will be the first Eastside city to consider changing that.

With no city minimum wage ordinance, Kirkland’s workers — like others in Eastside cities — are stuck with Washington’s floor of $17.13 per hour instead of the much higher wage floors in Seattle, unincorporated King County, the cities of SeaTac, Tukwila, Burien, Renton, and even Everett. These vary, but range to $3 to $4.50 per hour more.

Kirkland needs to fill in the gap. Raising the wage floor can be the difference between working one or two jobs; paying rent or living in a car; eating or skipping meals; and forgoing medical care or prescriptions.

Despite this wage disparity, it costs far more to live on the Eastside. Kirkland rents run hundreds of dollars above Seattle’s or Renton’s. Most low-wage workers can’t compete for housing in a city with median household incomes over $150,000 and instead commute. Though Kirkland has been making real efforts with zoning, funding, and creative policies to provide more affordable housing, raising the wage floor is a necessary step to reduce the housing affordability gap. Homelessness in wealthy areas is largely driven by wages that can’t cover rent.

On October 6, Kirkland will be the first city on the Eastside to consider supporting the essential workers who serve the community by raising the minimum wage. In April, Councilmembers Amy Falcone and John Tymczyszyn moved a request to the City Manager to prepare a study of the minimum wage and suggest action options. The vote was 6 to 1.

The lone “no,” Jon Pascal, separately had requested a “competitiveness study to support Kirkland’s economic development goals.” The two studies were merged and will be released along with the City Manager’s options for action on Friday, Oct 2, just days before the Council meeting.

Councilmembers Falcone, Tymczyszyn, Neal Black, Jay Arnold, and Shilpa Prem all committed to raising the wage floor to the Seattle or King County levels when they ran for office. Their decisions on October 6 will be the first opportunity to demonstrate those commitments and their support for Kirkland’s essential workers.

Kirkland should adopt the minimum wage that King County applied in unincorporated areas where it has jurisdiction. The King County Council ordinance passed 6-2 in May 2024 with every Democrat’s vote, including the Eastside’s Sarah Perry and Claudia Balducci, both easily re-elected. Katie Wilson who led that campaign is now Seattle’s Mayor. Councilmember Girmay Zahilay, who championed it, has moved up to King County Executive, and is doubling down on its popularity by creating a new Office of Labor Standards.
Raising the minimum wage is a central pillar of the Democratic Party. Even Kirkland’s opposition candidates supported a local equivalent to King County’s in the last election! It’s hugely popular.

Kirkland should join King County’s wage floor phase-in . It gives small businesses (15 or fewer employees and annual gross revenue under $2 million) a multiyear runway – a $0.50c annual increase (plus inflation) until they reach parity in 2031. Small businesses are not exempted because their employees pay the same prices as others and have to compete for housing too. In Seattle, at $4 per hour higher than Kirkland, new restaurants keep opening, and predictions of closure, business flight, and unemployment have again proven wrong .

Raising the wage floor doesn't just help workers at or near the minimum. It has a ripple effect, lifting wages for those making several dollars above the new floor too. If Kirkland moves forward with an ordinance matching King County’s, other Eastside and Northshore cities become more likely to follow, improving life for tens of thousands.

There has never been a better time to act. The cost of food, gas, heat, healthcare, and all necessities has grown even more out of reach for low-income families. The affordability crisis has become the nation’s top public concern and is driving the Democratic Party’s effort to win back working class voters. The crisis also creates support for raising wages.

There is even greater urgency for the immigrants who make up a substantial share of the low-wage workforce. New immigration rules and ICE’s terror have already destabilized household incomes for many. And starting October 1, the GOP’s “Big Beautiful Bill” cuts begin stripping Washington State Medicaid (Apple Health) from entire categories of legal immigrants. In blue cities, public revulsion over these policies is fueling support for local action. Can Kirkland call itself a "Welcoming City” while failing to act on behalf of the essential workers and immigrants who live or work there?

Finally, the framing of the forthcoming merged study likely pits raising poverty level wages against Kirkland’s economic vitality. Reality has consistently proven this to be a false dichotomy. We’re old enough to remember the “studies” and predictions of calamity when Seattle considered its minimum in 2014. They were false. We would still be awaiting child labor protections, collective bargaining rights, Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid if similar fearmongering had been heeded by elected officials. Seattleite Nick Hanauer’s recent article in The Atlantic shreds this framing.
Kirkland’s City Council has the opportunity to ease the burden of poverty for thousands of hardworking people. They should embrace it.

articles.title: Councilmembers Seek to One-Up Katie Wilson on Police Spending
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: After Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson’s 2027 proposed budget was released last week, the focus shifted to the Seattle City Council, some members of whom have made it clear during several days of meetings with City department heads that they are not happy with the proposal in front of them.

Councilmembers’ ire stands in stark contrast to the response of Seattle’s business community , who have been cautiously supportive of Wilson’s budget plan. Wilson deftly sidestepped a large amount of potential criticism from business interests with her focus on addressing the City’s structural budget deficit while not raising significant new taxes and increasing investment in the Seattle Police Department (SPD). Indeed, some might say she came out looking like the adult in the room , which was clearly a deliberate strategy on her part.

But Wilson’s fiscal responsibility has left less room for the Seattle City Council to maneuver in the last budget season before the majority of councilmembers (six, since Councilmember Debora Juarez will be stepping down before the end of the year) are up for reelection.

In an effort to close the $175 million budget deficit as well as to keep the budget deficit-clear through 2030, Wilson chose to discontinue the majority of one-time spending that was pervasive in 2026’s budget. This strategy marks a departure from the budget ethos practiced by her predecessor, Bruce Harrell, as well as upsetting the councilmembers who added most of those one-time investments without finding ongoing funds to continue them past this year.

City Budget Office Director Aly Pennucci told the council in one of their budget meetings this week that across the General and Jumpstart payroll tax funds, the 2026 budget spent $78 million in these one-time budget adds. Wilson’s proposal only continued $10-15 million of these investments, converting them into ongoing expenses for the City.

That being said, councilmembers weren’t even always happy about the investments that were maintained from last year, with Budget Chair Dan Strauss expressing displeasure that Wilson had made $4 million in one-time food bank and meal delivery investments from 2026 ongoing. Strauss said the Mayor’s Office should have consulted privately with councilmembers first. These investments were prioritized last year in anticipation of federal SNAP cuts contained in H.R. 1 – cuts that remain in place today.
“We provide as much food, money for food security as possible with the understanding that providing food is not a chartered responsibility,” Strauss said.

Councilmember ire aside, presenting this more sustainable budget was not without its pain points for Wilson. Most notably, her budget proposal transfers $65 million of 2026 dollars from the Seattle Office of Housing (OH). This money has already been allocated to housing projects, but Mayor’s Office told The Urbanist the impacted projects will still receive their awarded funding on the same timeline.

While this budget move has been sold as a way to allow the OH’s base budget to continue “substantially unchanged” in 2027-2028, it does ultimately amount to $65 million fewer dollars invested in housing, as the Mayor’s Office has told The Urbanist they don’t anticipate restoring the funds in the 2027-2028 biennium.

“This action does mean that there will be $65 [million] less overall invested in affordable housing in the long term, but we do not anticipate this action will have an impact on the availability of funding for new construction or the pace of construction in the near term,” said Alex Hudson, a spokesperson for the Mayor’s Office.

$65 million bears a striking resemblance to a few other investments in the 2027 proposed budget: namely, the $65 million of Jumpstart funds being allocated to homelessness response for the first time and the $68 million total increase to SPD’s budget. When choosing which investment to cut to balance the budget, Wilson chose affordable housing.

“This is a strategy that the Mayor's Office and the Budget Office put forward, and working in partnership with the Office of Housing, and they're being very thoughtful in thinking through how to actually implement this change,” Pennucci said during the OH’s presentation to the council. “What we see this as is an opportunity to both maintain the ongoing investments in affordable housing and frankly preserve many other investments across the budget in key areas.”
One of these investments is clearly SPD, although at least a few councilmembers still aren’t satisfied.
Wilson’s proposed budget increases SPD’s budget by a total of $68 million.

The Seattle Police Officers Guild (SPOG) contract that passed last December, in addition to the SPOG contract before that, gave huge raises to SPD’s rank and file, in addition to event overtime bonuses and additional salary premiums for education and language proficiency. This contract, along with new contracts with the Seattle Police Management Association (SPMA) and the Seattle Parking Enforcement Officers' Guild (SPEOG), are by far the greatest driver of the increased SPD budget, costing the City an additional $57.8 million in 2027.

Public safety chair Bob Kettle acknowledged this cost driver while failing to take any accountability for it, even though he voted for the new SPOG contracts in 2024 and 2025. Instead, he blamed the previous council.

“From a budget perspective, the SPOG agreement hurts from budgeting, just like when the Trump administration does different things that impact inflation. That hurts from a budget perspective,” Kettle said. “We were not set up for success in those agreements because of the bad decisions and the legacy of decisions made a half decade ago plus in this chamber.”
Kettle quickly added that he didn’t blame Councilmembers Debora Juarez and Strauss, who both served on that previous council.

Wilson also added $12.6 million to pay for staffing SPD up to 1,250 officers, a number that is then maintained through 2030. While SPD will receive the money for this full number in 2027, according to their own chart, they aren’t expected to actually reach 1,250 until November, meaning there might be some salary savings available for the department to try to reallocate elsewhere.

Due to the SPOG contract, SPD’s overtime budget will continue to grow with an additional $12.6 million being added compared to the 2026 budget. SPD’s overtime has ballooned in recent years, as is illustrated from this SPD chart from June. A new 2027 line added to the chart would read $62,000,000, about a 135% increase from 2022.

SPD is taking a few cuts in 2027 as well: namely, around $2.4 million to its media marketing budget, $467,000 to its hiring incentives budget, and the loss of many vacant positions (and two filled ones) for a savings of at least $5.7 million. However, none of the position cuts impacted command staff.
“The proposed budget does not include any abrogation or un-funding of command staff positions in SPD,” Hudson told The Urbanist .
Certain councilmembers were upset by almost all of these cuts.
Kettle was unhappy with the staffing numbers, saying he’d been told by “an expert in the area” that by 2050, Seattle will need 1,800 officers.

“It seems like we've given up on the goal of reaching 1,400 plus [officers], which is really the minimum that we need to have for officers,” Kettle said. “In fact, the proposed budget for 2028 is a sustainment budget that has zero new net hires. And should we, as a council, interpret this to mean that the Mayor's Office no longer wishes to grow the size of the deployment long term?”
Pennucci said that goal wasn’t grounded in financial reality.
“If there is a different choice, you need to reduce spending in other places to continue to grow beyond that number,” Pennucci said.

Interim SPD budget director Dan Eder said that right now, it costs a little over $200,000 to fund one officer position for a year, meaning that reaching the 1,450 officer number Kettle wants would cost more than $40 million in additional salary spendings every year…at least until another SPOG contract is negotiated, which will almost certainly push that number even higher.
Kettle was also upset that hiring bonuses for lateral officer hires from other police departments are being discontinued.

Councilmembers Juarez and Joy Hollingsworth both recited numbers of recent shooting fatalities and injuries in Seattle. Meanwhile, the SPD crime dashboard shows that citywide shootings and shots fired are down 28% year-to-date. Looking at the summer months (June-September) from the last several years, shootings and shots fired are down 103 incidents, around 36%, from their peak in the summer of 2023.

Councilmember Rob Saka led the charge on being upset about the lack of funding for surveillance cameras at the Seattle Center, which he expressed by standing up, taking a printed copy of the entire budget book, and dropping it on the dais.

“After the tragedy at the Bite, I expected this proposed budget to include funding for CCTV cameras at the Seattle Center,” Saka said. “As currently proposed, it does not. I find that omission extraordinarily difficult to understand, and incredibly disappointing.”

The facts of the shooting at the Bite of Seattle clearly illustrate that CCTV cameras at the site operated by SPD wouldn’t have done anything to prevent the outbreak of gun violence. SPD officers were within 100 feet of the shooting when it happened, and they had one shooter in custody within 30 seconds.

Councilmember Maritza Rivera was unhappy because she said the budget doesn’t contain funding for a focused deterrence strategy, a strategy that she spoke about at length during both the SPD and Community Assisted Response and Engagement (CARE) department presentations to council.

Pennucci corrected Rivera, saying there is about $300,000 in the budget each year for ongoing program evaluation, focused deterrence programs, and direct investments related to gun violence prevention.

Meanwhile, the Seattle Fire Department (SFD) is taking a 17% cut ($7.1 million) to its overtime budget, which will continue the unit outages that the department has already been experiencing. Most of the councilmembers expressed concern about this cut, while Pennucci defended the decision.

“The percent of the general fund that goes to the fire department is the second highest investment that we have in the city, and there are challenges,” Pennucci said. “They are managing unit outages today due to staffing challenges. We started at a much higher number when we were facing a more difficult situation prior to the revenue forecasts and other things. We worked really hard to get this [cut] down as low as possible, and there have been years where there have been significant unit outages that have fluctuated over the years, so it is a challenge. We are very confident in the ability for our fire department to manage this reduction, and it is an area we will continue to be working on.”

As Pennucci stated, SFD has already been facing unit outages due to staffing issues, although the department is making progress in improving their staffing numbers after the Covid-19 vaccine mandate caused many firefighters to leave. SFD is used to using a large amount of overtime, as can be seen from an analysis of the department’s 2024 overtime performed by PubliCola , which found many fire employees working thousands of hours of unevenly distributed overtime.
SFD Chief Scoggins said this overtime change in the 2027 budget will mean daily staffing will drop from 222 to 209 per day, impacting response times.

Councilmember Eddie Lin pointed out that the department’s new hires should alleviate overtime use, and Scoggins agreed that they are helping. Plus, since SFD’s budget includes funded positions that aren’t yet filled, there should be some salary savings coming into play as well.

articles.title: Scarecrow Video’s 2026 Psychotronic Challenge: Week One
articles.author: Julianne Bell and Audrey Vann
paras: Welcome to October! It’s the most wonderful time of the year, when I mitigate my seasonal depression by going all in on gothic literature and horror films. The good people at the world’s best video store, Scarecrow Video, have put together their 2026 Psychotronic Challenge , which contains 31 prompts for a movie each day throughout the month.
The rules are simple: watch at least one film each day that falls under the psychotronic category “in whatever order suits you,” and “have fun and get weird.”

Scarecrow defines “psychotronic” as “denoting or relating to a genre of films that typically have a science fiction, horror, or fantasy theme and were made on a low budget.” But the staff also notes that they don’t necessarily subscribe to the “low budget” definition in order to allow more diversity in the selection. “That being said,” they write, “we do like an underdog more often than not” so “you might as well have a lot of fun pushing yourself to new lows.”

My colleague Audrey Vann and I compiled a list of our picks for the first week to kick things off. Stay tuned for weekly posts with suggestions throughout the month. Support your local video store, and happy viewing! JULIANNE BELL
“This season’s opener will have some kind of seeking, stalking, tracking, or trapping, you know… hunting! Tally ho!”

This 1982 black comedy stars real-life BFFs—gay icon Paul Bartel and former Warhol superstar Mary Woronov (aka my mommy and daddy)—who appeared in 17 films together, including Rock ‘n’ Roll High School , Chopping Mall , and Death Race 2000 . In Eating Raoul, the duo plays a prudish couple, Paul and Mary Bland, who are just as broke as they are disgusted with evil sinners. One evening, Mary is attacked by a drunken swinger who stumbles into their apartment. She swiftly kills the man in self-defense, then checks his pockets to find wads of cash. The couple then mastermind a money-making scheme by luring “rich perverts” to their apartment (which, by the way, is filled with 1950s furniture—a very John Waters-esque detail) with personal ads, murdering them, taking their money, then throwing them into the trash compactor. The film ends with a memorable dinner-party scene that explains why it’s called Eating Raoul .
More ideas: The Night of the Hunter (1955), Black Christmas (1974), The Blair Witch Project (1999), Ready or Not (2019) , The Birds (1963), Perfect Blue (1997)
2. THATS COOKED: “Has to have a cooking scene, could be food or drugs or Soylent Green (oops, we burned that one for you).”

French director Julia Ducournau has my heart forever thanks to her freaky girl-meets-car body horror feature Titane , which I recommended for the Psychotronic Challenge back in 2024 . In her 2016 film Raw , lifelong vegetarian Justine (Garance Marillier) heads to vet school and, after being forced to eat rabbit kidneys via a hazing ritual, accidentally develops a taste for human flesh. Famously, some viewers required medical attention after fainting at the Toronto International Film Festival screening in 2016—don’t say we didn’t warn you!
More ideas: Fresh (2022), The Menu (2022), The Substance (2024) , Swallow (2019) , Bad Taste (1987) , Eating Raoul (1982)
3. STAKE HOUSE: “Wouldn’t that be a great name for a lumber yard run by a vampire? Ah ah ah.” Julianne’s pick: Bram Stoker’s Dracula (1992)

Francis Ford Coppola’s Bram Stoker’s Dracula has everything you could want in a gothic vampire movie: lush Academy Award-winning period costumes from designer Eiko Ishioka, Winona Ryder, Keanu Reeves as a guileless himbo doing a legendarily bad accent, dangerous levels of horniness, the iconic line “I have crossed oceans of time to find you,” stunning practical effects, Winona Ryder again. It’s become something of a fall tradition for me, and I invite you to steal it as your own.
More ideas: Sinners (2025), The Velvet Vampire (1971), Let’s Scare Jessica to Death (1971), Nosferatu the Vampyre (1979), Vampyros Lesbos (1971), Daughters of Darkness (1971)
4. BLOODLINE: “Must have ‘blood’ in the title.”

Promoted as Andy Warhol’s Dracula , Paul Morrissey’s vampiric tale is best known for its association with the famed artist, who, when asked about his contribution to the film, responded , “I go to the parties.” This one has everything a good movie should have: women in ghostly nightgowns, the sexiest man alive (Joe Dallesandro), hypnotism, and socialist propaganda.
More ideas: Blood & Black Lace (1964), Lady Snowblood (1973), The Blood on Satan’s Claw (1971), Blood Tea and Red String (2006), The Blood Splattered Bride (1972)
5. SHARK DAY: Weeks are for the weak, one day will do ya.
Audrey’s pick: Orca: The Killer Whale (1977)

Before you say “Cheater! That’s not a shark movie!” Let me clear up that there are, indeed, sharks at the beginning of this film. But more importantly, there are orcas, which are arguably scarier than sharks because of their intellect. (Orcas have actually been known to hunt great white sharks and eat their livers, but I digress.) The 1977 film Orca: The Killer Whale is about a male orca seeking revenge on a fishing boat whose captain unintentionally killed its pregnant mate. Sound familiar? That’s because this movie is a complete rip-off of Jaws , which came out two years prior. The film’s producer Dino de Laurentiis actually admitted to having seen Jaws and instructed screenwriter Luciano Vincenzoni to “find a fish tougher and more terrible than the great white.”
More ideas: Deep Blue Sea (1999) , Piranha (1978) , Jaws 3-D (1983) , Shark! (1969) , Cyclone (1978)
6. YOU CAN RUN BUT YOU CAN’T TIDE: “Sometimes the beach ain’t all sand and shine…”

I watched Sam Raimi’s survival horror thriller Send Help immediately post-surgery, while hopped up on painkillers, and had a damn blast. Rachel McAdams plays frumpy, awkward corporate strategist Linda Liddle, who gets stranded on a remote island with the company’s slimy, shallow CEO Bradley Preston ( Teen Wolf star Dylan O’Brien). While Linda thrives and becomes a beach goddess in this new environment due to her survival savvy, Preston flounders, and under this role reversal, their tense relationship takes a series of unexpected turns. Silly, gory, twisted, cathartic fun!
More ideas: The Fog (1980), I Know What You Did Last Summer (1997), Old (2021), Blood Beach (1980), The Sand (2015)
7. S.E.A. IT TO BELIEVE IT: “See a thing from South East Asia. Have you perused our newly minted Indonesian Horror section yet?”

This Malaysian indie coming-of-age horror film follows 12-year-old Zaffan, who is ridiculed for being the first of her classmates to go through puberty. With each act of shaming, rejection, and bullying, Zaffan goes from vibrantly social to shyly self-conscious and, eventually, powerfully monstrous.
More ideas: Kisapmata (1981), Ghost in the Cell (2026), Satan’s Slaves (2017), Dangerous Seductress (1992)
The post Scarecrow Video’s 2026 Psychotronic Challenge: Week One appeared first on The Stranger .

articles.title: Free Will Astrology
articles.author: Rob Brezsny
paras: ARIES (March 21-April 19): Orchids may lure pollinating insects with ingenious illusions rather than nectar. Some mimic the look or fragrance of other flowers. Others resemble female insects so convincingly that hopeful males unknowingly assist with pollination. From this, we might conclude that nature can be as duplicitous as humans. But rather than being bummed out by the facts of life, let’s use this as a lesson for you to wield in the coming days. Appearances can be deceiving—for both better and worse. If a situation initially seems disappointing or confusing, linger before drawing conclusions. Likewise, if something looks irresistibly attractive at first glance, investigate further. I predict your intuition will be extra skilled at distinguishing authentic richness from glamorous distraction.

TAURUS (April 20-May 20): I propose we make 93-year-old Taurus musician Willie Nelson your patron saint and role model for the foreseeable future. Earthy, unflappable, and unhurried, he has kept making his distinctive, soulful music for over 70 years, devoted all the while to the land and the people who work it. He has never pushed to sound like anyone else; he has patiently, inexorably become more fully himself. It’s your birthright to live like Nelson, Taurus, with a steady, sensual, enduring devotion to what you love. In the coming weeks, I invite you to tend to your deepest roots.

GEMINI (May 21-June 20): I may be preaching to the choir here, but there’s a fun kind of magic that thrives when you decline to be consistent. You Geminis are least likely, of all the signs, to exhaust yourself in trying to maintain a unified self-presentation. Like the Gemini poet Walt Whitman, you’re often pleased with the fact that you contain multitudes. It’s a potential superpower! The you who loves solitude and the you who craves connection can both be true. The skeptic and the mystic can coexist in the same nervous system. Your assignment: Honor three contradictory impulses without trying to make them coherent. You’re boisterously excused from having to make too much sense.

CANCER (June 21-July 22): In certain caves, like the Cave of the Crystals in Naica, Mexico, crystals grow to astonishing sizes. Why? Because the environment remains stable for thousands of years, with steady temperatures, minimal disturbances, and slow mineral flow. Under these stable conditions, ordinary molecules assemble into lavish structures. I believe you’re cultivating a similar sanctuary, Cancerian, as you invoke the powers of steadiness and devoted dedication. Even if progress appears slow, the underlying process is gradually generating a beautiful strength and/or lasting treasure. Now’s a good time to redouble your faith in your good work.

LEO (July 23-Aug. 22): The cosmic powers have granted you a license to be magnificent. Not arrogant, please note, but majestic, resplendent, and marvelous. You know the difference, right? Arrogance is parasitic, demanding that everyone reflects your glory back at you. Magnificence is expansive, making everyone feel more vital and attuned to their own splendor. The second option is far more nutritious and delicious for you in the long run. In the coming eons, and especially now, I hope you’ll be lavish with your praise and generous with your attention. Glow and dazzle in ways that inspire others to glow and dazzle.

VIRGO (Aug. 23-Sept. 22): A Zen teaching says, “Before enlightenment, chop wood, carry water. After enlightenment, chop wood, carry water.” But being the post-Zen teacher I am, I protest and say, “No, the chopping and the carrying ARE the enlightenment. There is no separate ‘after.'” The sacred is ALWAYS lurking in the mundane, disguised as ordinary tasks. And you Virgos are potentially the zodiac’s supreme master of this controversial truth. Others may chase after astral bling and transcendent glitter, but you know that divinity lives in the earthy details that are right in front of you. That’s how you transmute seemingly unremarkable stuff into the sublime. It’s time to wield your superpower to the hilt, please!

LIBRA (Sept. 23-Oct. 22): Let’s make Libran writer Ursula K. Le Guin your patron saint. She believed that any human arrangement, however permanent it seems, was made by people and can therefore be unmade and remade by people. The divine right of kings once seemed eternal and inevitable, she liked to remind us. Be like her in the coming weeks, Libra. Refuse to accept that the way things are is the way they must continue to be. Imagine more beautiful, more just, and more loving arrangements in every area of your life, including your relationships, your work, and your inner life. Then take three steps toward making it so.

SCORPIO (Oct. 23-Nov. 21): Volcanologists distinguish between two different eruptions. In the effusive type, lava flows slowly and steadily, while the explosive eruptions eject material fast and hard. What does this have to do with you? In my astrological estimation, you currently contain building pressures that need release. Here’s the good news: You can maneuver yourself in the direction of effusive expression and thereby make the explosive kind unnecessary. So my advice is to find small, controllable outlets for what’s gathering inside you. Don’t wait until the only option is a massive, sudden discharge.

SAGITTARIUS (Nov. 22-Dec. 21): You’ll flourish in the coming years if you ask daring questions and befriend sweet ambivalence and welcome adorable uncertainty. You’ll stumble upon weird but interesting success and project potent authenticity if you let your curiosity lead you to situations outside of your cozy bubbles and velvet ruts. On the other hand, you’ll flounder if you cling to folk wisdom foisted on you by the algorithms, treat all your opinions as facts, or pretend you always know what the f*ck is going on in this dazzling mess of a world. Keep it generous and exploratory, Sagittarius. Seek out wide-ranging conversationalists and playful skeptics.

CAPRICORN (Dec. 22-Jan. 19): A river delta is where a river finally meets the sea. Instead of arriving as one bold channel, it fans out into dozens of branching streams, depositing the rich silt it has carried for many miles. Deltas are fertile places because of everything the river gathered along the way and finally lays down. You’re approaching a metaphorical delta, Capricorn. All the experiences, emotions, and impressions you’ve been carrying are ready to be released and turned into fertile ground. Abundance wants to grow from all you’ve gathered.

AQUARIUS (Jan. 20-Feb. 18): In the 17th century, Aquarian astronomer Johannes Hevelius mapped the moon with surprising accuracy. Yet he worked with funky homemade telescopes perched on a homemade observatory that he built on the rooftops of his three connected houses. I recommend you borrow his approach, Aquarius. You might feel tempted to postpone action until conditions are ideal, but I hope you’ll begin with what you already possess. Prediction: As you proceed, your tools and strategies will evolve. Momentum will become one of your key resources.

PISCES (Feb. 19-March 20): In traditional Chinese medicine, wei qi is a protective energy that circulates beneath the skin, forming a shield against harmful influences. To nourish it, you revel in sleeping and eating well. You work diligently, with tender discernment, to maintain healthy boundaries. How are you doing with that, Pisces? Is it possible you’ve been working so hard on your deep transformations that you’ve semi-neglected this outer layer of strength? I hope that in the coming weeks, you’ll nurture the subtle shields that prevent you from absorbing every stray particle of psychic weirdness in your environment. Think of this task not as building walls, but tending to your garden’s edges.

paras: More than 10,000 refugees, asylum-seekers, and other lawful immigrants in Washington are losing their healthcare, starting today , thanks to language in Donald Trump’s House Resolution 1 (aka that monstrous “One Big Beautiful Bill”), in which people with certain immigration statuses are no longer eligible for Medicaid or Apple Health in Washington. Please remember to vote in the midterms. They are next month! Despite Trump’s best efforts, mail-in voting is still intact. Please. We’ve gotta regain control of the House, the Senate, anything and everything that could result in us impeaching this motherfucker. Again.

In related news, the Supreme Court will review Trump’s policy that denies bond hearings for immigrants, according to the Associated Press . “Most appeals courts to have considered the issue have found that it violates federal law to detain immigrants, including those living in the U.S. illegally, without a bond hearing.” Court is back in session Monday.

Trump’s new ad, being created in-house by the White House video team and being paid for by taxpayers, is an absolute mess and even some of his supporters think so. One former campaign official told CNN , “This is dumb, dumb, dumb beyond belief. These guys are all gonna get subpoenaed. It’s gonna be bad.” Hardly the worst thing they’ve ever done, but it’s nice to see them be publicly touted as idiots.

Here comes a Kelvin wave! What’s a Kelvin wave, you ask? It’s a “giant pulse of warm water,” and it’s coming for the West Coast. The wave is expected to hit California in a matter of days and, according to the Seattle Times , it may raise sea levels by half a foot or more, possibly for the next several months. Kelvin waves have already hit the California coast in the spring, but this one’s supposed to be bigger. Could make for some interesting sea creature spotting ! It’s not expected to impact the Washington coast.

Defund cops; fund art! Did you read Amanda Manitach’s story about the open letter to Mayor Katie Wilson in which local artists, business owners, and organizers call for Wilson to divert $8 million from SPD’s proposed $68 million budget increase and give that money to the arts? It’s a great idea! Read all about it .

Tennessee attempted to execute Christa Pike yesterday and failed. Pike was administered two doses of pentobarbital, but witnesses say she could be heard snoring more than an hour after the injection. Pike was taken to the hospital, and her lawyers say she’s still alive. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has suspended all remaining 2026 executions as a result; Gary Sutton was scheduled to be executed on December 3. This is the second botched attempt at lethal injection in Tennessee this year. In May, the state had to cancel the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers after taking more than an hour to place an IV line. Gov. Lee granted Carruthers a one-year reprieve. The system’s working great. No notes.

Bats! A Puyallup elementary school has a bat problem , and they’ve called in professionals to help. The school has found six bats in its halls this year. Maybe they just want to learn some things! Leave ‘em be!

Courtney Stodden did it. Remember Courtney Stodden? The 16-year-old who married 51-year-old actor Doug Hutchison, and participated in an absolutely unhinged press tour that included being examined by Dr. Drew on his show Dr. Drew’s Lifechangers to see if her boobs were real? We as a society did her dirty, and she’s been rightfully calling us out on it for years. She was a child, she was groomed, and she wasn’t protected by her parents. (Scaachi Koul wrote a great profile on her in 2019 to catch you up.) Since leaving her marriage, Stodden, 32, has been working to make child marriage illegal in America. Her latest victory is California, which just outlawed marriage for anyone under 18, even with parental permission.
A judge has “permanently dismissed” charges against David Hearn, the former Olympic slalom canoeist charged with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
In other lawsuit news, Renee Good’s family is suing the government and several immigration officials . Godspeed.

News is still coming out about the seven Cornell students who allegedly raped a young woman for hours in 2024 and walked away with the equivalent of a slap on the wrist. The student victim, Jane Doe, talked to campus police for hours. Campus police condensed her interview into a statement that suggested she consented to everything. Police sent that condensed statement to a prosecutor, who decided not to press charges. But the New York Times has obtained documents that suggest that the condensed statement omitted vital details, including Jane Doe saying, “There was really no escape,” and “ I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped .” I have lost track of how many people have failed Jane Doe within this horrific story.

Please take care of yourselves. A lot of the news is not good right now! And if you find yourself reeling in the endless nightmare, please log off. Go for a walk. Today is going to be partly cloudy and 65 degrees, and all the leaves are starting to turn, so it’s really pretty outside, pretty much everywhere. And today, if you need a treat, the Pastry Project is hosting a soft serve pop-up with special fall flavors from 3–9 p.m. No, ice cream doesn’t fix anything. But smiling can literally release endorphins and happy brain chemicals like dopamine and serotonin, and it’s hard not to smile while eating delicious ice cream and looking at colorful trees.
