articles.title: Pinehurst Station Bursts into Action, as Upzones Trail Behind
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Today, Pinehurst Station is officially a stop on both the 1 Line and 2 Line, bringing another Seattle neighborhood into the fold of the region's growing light rail system. Trains began stopping at Pinehurst bright and early at the start of service: 4:57am to be exact.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in final stretch! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us blow past our goal!

Pinehurst's opening day arrived five years sooner than the Sound Transit 3 (ST3) ballot measure pledged in 2016. The station's arrival and accelerated timeline is thanks to a concerted push from Seattle activists and leaders. Local organizer Renee Staton recounted that journey in a recent guest piece in The Urbanist .

The infill light rail station had been left on the cutting room floor as ST2 plans were formulated in 2008, but ST3 secured funding for the project with a 2031 opening targeted. Pinehurst ended up coming in at a cost of $240 million.

"Now, 2016, the region approved this station as part of Sound Transit 3, and we, at that time, operated 21 stations across 22 miles of track," Constantine said Tuesday. "Well, this station will be the 30th station we have opened since then. While almost tripling the track mileage, we'll now have 51 stations and 63 miles of track. That is a phenomenal pace of growth, and this is a system that our region has embraced wholeheartedly."

Sound Transit board members were convinced of the wisdom of opening the station shortly after the Lynnwood Link extension grand opening, voting to accelerate the timeline in 2020 and finalizing that decision a year later. Beyond simply wanting to deliver the station to North Seattle communities sooner, a practicality and cost-effectiveness argument swayed some votes. Construction costs tend to only climb with time, while fitting in construction windows becomes more difficult as ridership grows.

Lynnwood Link construction laid the track and the basic structure of the station, and some additional work happened before Lynnwood Link officially opened, though there were also significant disruptions to existing riders to get the station fully built after service commenced.

With the extension of the 2 Line across Lake Washington in March, regional light rail ridership has taken a big leap. Daily ridership exceeded 160,000 in April and continued to grow over the summer, spiking at a one-day record of 309,000 during Seattle's last World Cup match in July. This growth appears to have made Sound Transit the most-ridden light rail system in America – though several heavy rail metros have higher ridership.

The agency hosted a ribbon-cutting ceremony for its new infill station Tuesday afternoon, featuring a smorgasbord of speeches from local officials. Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson gave a nod to the leadership from transit advocates and Councilmember Debora Juarez (who wasn't in attendance) to make the station happen, and to the work ahead to make Graham Street infill station happen in Southeast Seattle.

"This is South Transit's first infill station, but it certainly will not be the last, and it happens because the people fought for it," Wilson said. "So thank you to Councilmember Juarez and all of the community advocates who made sure that Pinehurst did not get left behind. And thank you to the Sound Transit Board and agency for listening and delivering."

To the south in the Rainier Valley, Graham Street very nearly did not survive Sound Transit's "Enterprise Initiative" expansion plan overhaul in May. Board Chair Dave Somers proposed tabling the project indefinitely, but Wilson spearheaded a push to keep it on track to open around 2031. It ended up taking the pledge of $30 million in last-in funding from the City of Seattle to avoid the chopping block.

Located between Northgate and South Shoreline, Pinehurst Station is projected to attract 2,600 to 4,200 boardings daily boardings – at least once the system and surrounding neighborhood matures. That ridership would be on par with Mountlake Terrace (also near a golf course) and Beacon Hill. The late September opening coincides with the start of classes at the University of Washington and meets the agency's goal of opening the station in the third quarter of the year.

The station happened on a faster timeline than Seattle's rezoning process for the surrounding neighborhoods. The city had almost looked ready to advance its overdue Comprehensive Plan update until legal appeals derailed the process , forcing additional analysis on top of an environmental study that was already 1,300 pages long.

As a result, Pinehurst Station is surrounded by single family homes, a fenced-off City-owned golf course, and of course an obligatory gaping freeway trench spewing noise and pollution in the general vicinity. While the Comprehensive Plan declined to tackle the latter two issues, it had queued up rezones allowing five- to eight-story apartment buildings and ground-floor retail in several swaths of Pinehurst and some more limited areas of Haller Lake, replacing some broad areas of low-density Neighborhood Residential zoning.
Wilson acknowledged the delay and her resolve to see the rezones though, which she has also sought to augment with her Taller Faster Denser Plan .

"This is not just a station; it is a spark – a spark for long-term transformation in the newly designated Pinehurst-Haller Lake Urban Center, where we will see more homes, shops, services, parks, and walkable streets, all connected to great transit. That's what it's all about," Wilson said. "Sometimes we build transit where lots of density already exists, and sometimes we build transit, and we're able to welcome people around them."

Councilmember Dan Strauss – who like Wilson sits on the Sound Transit Board – upped the ante and declared Pinehurst a prime candidate for a freeway lid to create more developable land near the station and reconnect the street grid. As it stands, the west side of the station is cut off by I-5, with no safe bike facility and an unpleasant experience for those walking and rolling. Shoreline is building a pedestrian bridge at its 148th Street Station, but Seattle has no such facility planned.

"As we pass the Comprehensive Plan, there is more density. And when we are looking to reconnect across I-5, I talked today with Office of Planning and Community Development about the needing to lid I-5," Strauss said. "We can do so without any public funds. It recreates the grid. It increases the property tax that King County and Seattle has, and we had it done in Washington D.C. for zero public financing. This is a perfect candidate, and I'll tell you, it would not have the oomph if it weren't for this station."

Councilmember Eddie Lin, who chairs the land use committee, told the Seattle Times that he thinks it might be 2028 before the council is fully able to enact zoning changes, due to the need for additional time-consuming environmental studies to resolve the legal challenges.

While the Growth Management Hearings Board threw out the environmental complaints levied against Seattle's waylaid growth plan, it did find that the document failed to sufficiently study a higher growth scenario than the 120,000 new housing units over 20 years that was the upper echelon of Harrell's proposal. This is much to the chagrin of housing advocates who specifically pushed the Harrell administration to include a higher growth scenario in the plan. Over the last decade, Seattle has often exceeded the 6,000 homes per year production pace in the growth plan.

The upshot of this planning snafu is that Pinehurst likely waits a few more years for the blanket ban on new apartments to be lifted across much of its walkshed. At that point, perhaps an infusion of new housing will happen if interest from builders is there.

The Seattle Department of Transportation did deliver a number of street upgrades in time for the opening, including a new roundabout, protected bike lanes connecting Lake City to the station, new greenways, and a shared-use path to James Baldwin Elementary. The roundabout at Roosevelt and 125th is the first full-sized roundabout ever built inside city limits.

"About 90% of riders are expected to arrive without a car," Wilson said. "That is remarkable, and it's exactly why we have been investing in safer streets, new sidewalks, protected bike lanes, upgraded bus stops, and better buses. And for the real transportation wonks out there, we are excited to open the first roundabout in Seattle at Roosevelt Way NE and NE 125th Street."

King County Metro added Route 77 in its last service change providing a feeder route for the station that finally offers a direct bus connection between Lake City and Bitter Lake. Route 77 features 15-minute frequencies from 7am to 8pm, before dropping to half-hour headways thereafter. Other neighborhoods are feeling shortchanged by the adjustments Metro has been making around light rail openings, after losing direct connections that they once had.

Similar to other Sound Transit stations, artwork has been a major focus when it comes to potential placemaking. Pinehurst's prominent station art was designed by Seattle-based artist Romson Bustillo , who was born on the island of Mindanao in the Philippines. Human and animal figures brightly patterned in red, yellow, and green give the station a South Pacific vibe.

The station opening today will mark the last light rail opening in the region for quite some time. Sound Transit will roll out its Stride bus rapid transit network in 2028 and 2029. For light rail openings, Graham Street is next on deck in 2031. West Seattle Link has slipped to 2035 , which is also when Sound Transit is expecting to open Tacoma Dome Link . The agency is hoping to launch the first leg of the Everett Link extension (as far as Paine Field) in 2037.

Ballard Link, meanwhile, has considerable uncertainty, with 2042 for the whole line the best case scenario, which would require closing a huge budget gap of around $8 billion. The less-rosy scenario would be opening only the downtown portion in the 2040s and delaying the Interbay and Ballard section to the 2060s , pending enough funding accruing in Sound Transit coffers.

Another looming cloud on the horizon is labor strife. A half dozen picketers turned out to the ribbon-cutting with signs demanding a fair labor deal. One of those picketing Sound Transit workers, Brian Vierela, said a group currently exempt from collecting bargaining and working in project control, environmental permitting, community outreach, and systems engineering are seeking to unionize under Protec17, but they say they are being given the run around from a CEO that just got a lucrative extension himself .

"We're very happy that [Pinehurst] is opening," Vierela told The Urbanist . "We want to come here and show support for all of the workers that made this possible. But we're also very frustrated at the negotiating table with Dow. Recently Dow was able to have his contract renewed in about you know a handful of hours of the board deliberating. We have been at the negotiating table for over 18 months at this point, and we're here to essentially ask Dow to get us a deal and respect our union, and let's just move forward."
Ballard Congratulates Golf Course on Its New Light Rail Station: tinyurl.com/yncw9jep [image or embed]

The struggle to get light rail to Ballard while many less populous and popular destinations are added to the system led the satire site The Needling to write the headline "Ballard Congratulates Golf Course on Its New Light Rail Station."

While rezones bringing density are inbound eventually, for now the satirical headline isn't far off. Mike Lindblom's station opening preview in the Seattle Times wasn't much more sanguine, framing the station as a potential boondoggle. Lindblom noted that if the land use around the station isn't able to improve by leaps and bounds, ridership could skew toward the low end of Sound Transit's projections – with as few as 1,100 daily riders hopping on trains.
King County Councilmember Rod Dembowski took the opportunity to respond directly to those claims Tuesday.

"I know, Mr. Lindblom, that you know based on your reporting, there are some doubts about ridership, whether this should have been built, whether the investment was worth it," Dembowski said. "I'm here to tell you, we are here, and it was worth it. This station is going to deliver on riders. It's going to deliver on housing. It's going to deliver for Lake City that needed this investment, and I encourage everyone to do what I did: take the 77, a beautiful, brand new bus that adds east-west connections to this part of the city."

articles.title: Seattle as the Fourth Best Global City? Oxford Economics Says So
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: It was the best times; it was the worst of times. Depending whom you ask, Seattle's economy is one of the most elite in the world, or it's on death's doorsteps and in the midst of a corporate exodus . Oxford Economics weighed in this week on the positive side of the ledger, ranking Seattle as the fourth best city in the world on its 2026 Global Cities Index , trailing only New York, London and Paris.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in the home stretch! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us exceed our goal!

"Seattle’s economic strength propels it to the fourth spot of our 2026 Global Cities Index," the report noted. "This is largely thanks to the city’s major tech sector—home to both Microsoft and Amazon—which rivals those of any other city in the world. The metro also boasts major players in other industries such as aerospace (Boeing) and is home to major retail headquarters (Starbucks, Costco, and Nordstrom). This range of large employers gives the city one of the highest levels of GDP per person in our index and a healthy economic diversity measure."

The report was a good reminder that much is relative in economic analysis. Case in point: Mayor Katie Wilson's administration recently released a report that stressed that Seattle's economy (and the governmental revenue streams that rely on it) is not currently diversified enough, relying too heavily on a tech sector that could pull up stakes, or convert to an AI robot workforce that leaves many locals out of a job. Wilson launched a Resilient Seattle Economy Task Force to work on the issue and craft a strategy to grow and diversify the local economy.

At a recent public appearance , Wilson noted it is tough to manage the tension of wanting to decrease income inequality and rein in big tech's power while not killing the golden goose that is paying a big chunk of the City of Seattle's bills. The campaign that swept Wilson into office was focused on affordability and the idea that Seattle's economic boom should be more broadly shared. That campaign touched on improving governance, quality life, and environmental stewardship.

While the global index seems geared toward indicating business opportunities to corporate leaders, Oxford Economics – a commercial advisory firm based in Oxford, England – notes the analysis goes beyond solely looking at economic output: "We score cities based on a range of metrics across five categories: Economics, Human Capital, Quality of Life, Environment, and Governance."

Oxford's authors pointed out that very high incomes can be a double-edged sword contributing to climbing housing prices, especially as housing supply lags – with Seattle's slow pace to easing zoning restrictions and other development hurdles partially to blame for that lag.

"The city scores favourably in the Quality of Life category as a concentration of high-value sectors results in Seattle residents having a very high income per person (fourth in the world). However, this can be a double-edged sword, as income inequality is also considerably high in the city. This is especially concerning as Seattle’s consistent population growth and limited housing supply are set to contribute to increasingly unaffordable house prices and rents."
Seattle had the second highest quality of life ranking in the United States (22nd globally), behind San Jose, California, which (perhaps bizarrely) ranked 13th in the globe.

Seattle's qualify of life was on full display on the international stage this summer as the city's downtown hosted six FIFA Men's World Cup matches and earned the city a distinction as a top host with a booming transit system , bustling pedestrian zone, and beautiful waterfront park. The Bay Area, meanwhile, trucked fans to distant Santa Clara to watch matches in suburban recluse mode. How's that for quality of life?

Seattle also generally outperforms the U.S. field when it comes to environmental footprint and climate pollution per capita , with a big credit going to policies limiting suburban sprawl and promoting housing growth in transit-rich areas. Plus, with perhaps the most ambitious transit expansion plans in the country, the Seattle metropolitan area is adding more transit-rich areas – albeit with some snags and delays along the way .

While Oxford Economics top 100 list is heavily weighted toward the Anglo world and Europe, authors do note that Asia is seeing some of fastest economic growth and is climbing the ranks. While pure GDP per capita (on which Seattle ranks 4th in the world at $152,000) seems the largest weight in the index, some cities climb the rankings due to quality of life, governance, and environmental factors, with European standouts often taking that route.

"Cities across North America and Europe dominate the top reaches of our index, with the US alone accounting for 30 of the top 100 cities," the report states. "Yet the drivers of this dominance between the two regions differs. In the US, it is strong scores across the Economics and Human Capital categories that drive their elevated position. In Europe, however, it is outperformance across the Quality of Life, Environmental, and Governance categories. These differences are emblematic of current trends and policy priorities, as the US continues to post strong economic gains, while Europe retains its advantage in resident amenities and liveability."

Another trend the report highlights is how Trump's erratic policymaking impacts the governance of American cities and the how its anti-immigrant policies could starve American cities of their lifeblood of talented immigrants that propel their economic engines. The authors ranked all U.S. cities 198th on governance, a swipe at the Trump administration, and they highlighted the threat that Trumpism posed to Seattle in particular.

"[T]he downside risk of the Trump administration’s immigration policies will likely limit international immigration to the city, reducing population growth and the share of foreign-born residents," the report said. "This may hold Seattle back from making gains in the Human Capital category in the next few years."

Beyond federal chaos, part of Seattle's governance challenge is high mayoral turnover. Wilson will likely seek to break the run of one-term mayors, but several members of the local mainstream media appear to have already turned against her, concocting negative headlines to the detriment of more positive stories that are out there, as this recent Oxford Economics report illustrates.

articles.title: The Northwest Film Forum Will Be Open Seven Days a Week
articles.author: Chase Hutchinson
paras: Lovers of weird, eclectic, and thoughtfully-programmed cinema rejoice! The Northwest Film Forum (NWFF), Seattle’s nonprofit independent art house cinema, is making a big expansion: starting Monday, they’ll be open for all seven days of the week.

This is the first time NWFF will be showing movies every day with a full staff. More than a decade ago, the organization had daily screenings, but that relied on volunteer labor. For the expansion, while they’ll still have volunteers, staff is running things and NWFF is bringing on additional projectionists to expand their team to cover evening screenings. It’s a far cry from 2024 when NWFF laid off nearly half its staff . Now, there will be no more “dark days” (when the theater was typically closed on both Monday and Tuesday) since the lights will be on all week long.

One reason for the operational expansion is because NWFF is thriving. The organization’s unique programming—a real fuck you to AI slop and the glut of algorithmically-driven streaming trash—is bringing in audiences. According to NWFF, attendance increased 62 percent between 2024 and 2025. And even though the fall movie season is just getting started, attendance this year is already up 27 percent from last year. With doors open every day, NWFF hopes those numbers will keep climbing.

Jill Busby, who took over as the full-time executive director at NWFF back in January, said NWFF had been considering expanding for a while. “Once we were seeing higher attendance, it felt really justified,” Busby says. They could pull this off. A lot of this recent success is due to NWFF’s programming. NWFF has never lacked for weird shit and a diversity of films. Just recently, they closed out the Local Sightings Film Festival with the North American premiere of the fascinating experimental documentary The Joyless Economy and are now opening the one-of-a-kind pseudo sci-fi horror film Chronovisor this weekend. While there is a team working on programming festivals and community groups that bring in their own films, Busby specifically credited NWFF director of exhibition Cole Wilder as being central to their growth, calling him a “programming wizard.”
In addition to more programming that will make the most active Letterboxd users rock hard, Busby says the expansion will open up the theater to the community.

“We also want to have the opportunity to do a diversity of events,” Busby says. “So more rentals, more partnerships, more weird shit. Whatever we can fit in there to be a more active space seven days a week.”

Building off those partnerships could mean more interesting local festivals like what NWFF is already hosting. Next month from Oct. 15-18, this will include the return of the Seattle Trans Underground Film Festival (STUFF) , which has proven to be one of the more exciting new festivals to burst onto the scene.

Now that they’re open seven days, not only will NWFF have more flexibility to hold screenings and events like these, they’ll also be able to potentially bring in films that require longer runs on what are known as “clean screens.” TLDR: A distributor can say “if you want this film, you need to play it for this amount of time on its own dedicated screen.” Now, if NWFF wants one of those films in the future, their increased capacity means they can meet that requirement.
The expansion is a testcase. A knock on wood. NWFF has seen audiences dry up (see: that pesky pandemic) and has been through the ringer before (see: those 2024 layoffs), but Busby is optimistic.
“We’re seeing this year how it goes and if it feels like it’s not working, we’ll be responsive to that,” Busby says. “But it probably will.”

It’s more good news for independent Seattle movie theaters. Earlier this month, the Grand Illusion Cinema announced it’s moving into the University District’s Varsity Theatre later this fall. And local organization WFLM has a deal in the works to take over the Egyptian Theatre which SIFF abandoned after declining to renew their lease around this time last year. Adding the NWFF’s expansion to the mix could foretell the start of a real turnaround for local movie theaters.

Whether this will usher in a new golden age for film heads remains to be seen. There are big challenges to running a theater. But after the last few years of empty seats and theater closures, there’s hope in the local scene.
“I do think we’re in a very good moment for moviegoing. Specifically in Seattle, I think we do have just a very big variety of stuff happening,” Wilder says. “I’m excited to see where things go.”

articles.title: Pop Loser: Where Are They Now? (Albino Burmese Python Edition)
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: Welcome back to Pop Loser! Spiritually, I’m in a place of the 2001 VMAs when Britney Spears debuted “I’m a Slave 4 U,” and apparently I’m not alone—the track is having a moment with Gen Z. I’ll dive into some herstory about the albino Burmese python from the famed VMAs performance. Plus, the 2026 VMAs happened this weekend, if you even care. And oh my god, Tinashe’s new album Popstar is perfect.
This week in Strangerland, I attended Lily Allen’s West End Girl tour at the Paramount on Thursday night, which was a masterclass in public shaming. Read my full review here.

On Friday, the Space Needle glowed pink in honor of Dolly Parton. The occasion marked Seattle’s first official Dolly Day, 9/25 (a reference to 9 to 5 ), which councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck announced last week. The Pacific Science Center, Lumen Field, the Great Wheel, and Columbia Tower also added touches of pink to the skyline in Parton’s honor.

Spiritually, I’m in a place of the 2001 VMAs, when Britney Spears debuted “I’m a Slave 4 U,” adorned in body glitter and dripping with sweat, with an albino Burmese python draped around her neck. And I’m not alone—according to Rolling Stone , new Spotify data shows that the 25-year-old song is trending amongst Gen Z. Fifty-five percent of global streams in the past month came from listeners born between 1997 and 2012. Twenty-seven percent of listeners were not even born when Spears debuted the song.

Fun fact: The celebrated serpent featured in the VMAs performance is apparently named “Banana,” something I learned back in 2006 when she was used in a photo shoot on America’s Next Top Model . MTV staff writer Crystal Bell tracked the python down in 2016 to confirm that the female snake was still alive and had, in fact, grown nearly four times larger; the owners estimated she weighed in at around 20 pounds in 2001 and had grown to roughly 100 pounds (and around 14 feet long). Personally, I need to see another 10-year update on Banana.

Speaking of the VMAs, that happened over the weekend (if you even care). Madonna opened the show (her first VMA performance in 23 years) with Sabrina Carpenter and Charli XCX (nobody kissed , unfortunately). There were also cameos from Julia Garner, Seth Rogen, Andrew Watt, Debi Mazar, Gabbriette, SOMBR, and Madonna’s ex, Tony Ward (who appears in music videos for “Cherish,” “Justify My Love,” and “Erotica”).

Other highlights from the 2026 VMAs included two very unrehearsed speeches from Madonna, who won Best Collaboration and Best Dance (and several other untelevised categories). When the Queen of Pop accepted the award for Best Dance, she feigned pulling a laser out of her ass, then remarked: “I’m kind of unclear what this award is for…” (It was for “Confessions II.”)

articles.title: Slog AM: Some in Seattle Felt that Earthquake, Repeal of Washington’s Millionaires Tax Is Polling Poorly, Sen. Amy Klobuchar Saves the Day
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: Seattle just can’t stop dying. The 2026 Global Cities Index by Oxford Economics clearly shows it has one foot in the grave. How else to explain the city being rated fourth in the whole fucking world when it comes to “economics, human capital, quality of life, environment, and governance.” What a catastrophe . Seattle is only behind Paris, London, and Mamdaniland. You got that right. The 206 beat big time players like San Francisco, Tokyo, Berlin, and Toronto. Why? Because of its exceptional concentration of “human capital,” which, in 2025, resulted in a metropolis with an impressive $632 billion GDP. Now think about this for a moment. That’s not far from Shanghai’s GDP ($816 billion). But that financial center has a population of 24 million. Our metropolitan area is just 4.1 million. Seattle, death becomes you.

Clearly, what our city needs is not more capitalism, we are filled to the gills with all of that stuff. What we really need is more socialism. We are way behind in that department. But when, say, Mayor Katie Wilson proposes expanding Seattle transit she must resort to a sales tax increase. What’s sad in all of this is the city, a super-rich city, can’t find any other way to fund something that’s so vital to its general well-being. In our town, there’s only money for making more money (M-M) and no money for making life livable for those whose “human capital” does not make the cash registers sing.

A quick note. The concept of “human capital” has an origin. It’s a 1964 book, Human Capital: A Theoretical and Empirical Analysis by Gary Becker, an economist who was part of the Chicago School of Economics. In short, he was a neoliberal. And the true (and even nefarious) goal of his human capital project was to convince wage earners (store attendants, mechanics, janitors, plumbers, bus drivers, you name it), that they were just like their exploiters: capitalists. A wage, in this view of things, was a return on your capital. And going to school was like a speculator investing in a new luxury tower. Even crossing the border sans-papiers was an investment on your capital. For this neoliberal nonsense, which was popularized in 2005 by the mind-numbingly dumb book Freakoconomics , Becker received a Nobel prize in economics in 1992.

A new statewide poll shows that the initiative to repeal Washington’s Millionaires Tax is in trouble. Seattle Times reports that 57 percent of voters rejected Initiative 645 when its fiscal hit on the state’s budget (cuts in healthcare and education) was explained, as opposed to 35 percent who, nevertheless, gave it a thumbs up. The supporters of the repeal of course do not want voters to know about this impact; they are desperate to keep the consequences in the dark. But that’s not going to happen. The needed fiscal information will appear on the ballot in November.

Did you feel that? I didn’t. The earthquake that happened near Port Orchard around 2:05 p.m. yesterday . I completely missed it. Though some claim they felt the ground move a little beneath their feet. So far, no damage to life and property has been reported.

Yesterday was perfect. Low and slow-moving clouds. Rain now and then. Leaves swirling in the wind. Wheeling birds above the trees. Lovers kissing on a wet sidewalk. Dogs in raincoats. Highs below 60. An early dusk. A longish night. A dream about a long-dead and mostly forgotten foe. Today will not be as nice. Dark clouds will not carry the sun away. Expect a high of 64.

Astronomers at the Roque de los Muchachos Astrophysical Observatory have identified the “ largest known galaxy .” Its name: IC 1101. Its distance from us: over a billion light-years. Its size: “wider than 17 Milky Ways lined up in a row.” Does that make you feel so small? Insignificant like a speck of dust? As trivial as a puff of smoke? If so, it would do you well to recall this line by America’s greatest poet, Emily Dickinson : “The Brain — is wider than the Sky — For — put them side by side — The one the other will contain / With ease — and You — beside —”

There is no doubt in my mind that Sen. Eric Schmitt knew exactly what he was doing, when, during a bogus Senate Judiciary Committee hearing concerning the investigation that followed Trump’s attempted coup on January 6, 2021, he asked the former special counsel Jack Smith if he attended an Atlanta Hawks game on February 3, 2024. Of course Smith said no; and of course Schmitt unrolled with the fervor and quickness of an ejaculating demon some conspiracy theory concerning an encounter with Fani Willis, the Black district attorney of Fulton County, Georgia. (Both rightly went after Trump for breaking the law.) Schmitt claimed he had text messages from Smith’s team that proved he went to the game, accused him of perjury, went on about the Soviet Union, and finally called him a “total dirtbag.” And that was the whole point. Schmitt had nothing more to say. He wanted to move on. He put suspicion in the air. Mainstream media would take care of the rest: Smith Met Willis During a Hawks Game? And it would likely stick, despite the lack of evidence. But then came the surprise and what must be one of the most comic moments in the history of Senate hearings.

Thanks to the tenacity of Sen. Amy Klobuchar it was eventually revealed that Jack Smith had been to a basketball game on February 3 , but it was in Maryland, and involved the Iowa Hawkeyes, a college women’s basketball team, not the Atlanta Hawks, a professional men’s team. The conspiracy theory died almost as soon as it was born. And what the dodo senator from the Show-Me State, Schmitt, exposed instead was yet another great waste of taxpayers’ money. This hearing, that ballroom, the helipad, Trump’s tax-funded political ad, and so on and so on. What we see day after day is the brazen blazing of public cash.

Ain’t that America. Arkansas’ governor, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, made an ad that said the usual kind of right-wing crap: people don’t work because they are too lazy, and so welfare is just a waste of taxpayers’ money. But here is the thing: her example of a lazy welfare recipient was a young white male eating snacks and playing video games in a dark room. This depiction apparently upset her base because it was further evidence of the persecution of white males in our society. They have it so, so bad. And this ad only made matters worse. It would have been better, and more accurate, if Sanders showed black males with their pants sagging or black women with too many babies. A comment on X: “Our government has systematically discriminated against white males for decades now, and yet now has the audacity to dishonestly mock young white males as welfare queens.” Even if it’s true, which it’s not, you are still talking about decades? What about 400 years of slavery? In the words of Burning Spear: “Do you remember the days of slavery. How they worked us so hard.”
In fact, let’s end AM with Burning Spear’s Slavery Days .

articles.title: Amtrak Airo Sneak Peak
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: The newest trains in Amtrak’s fleet, Amtrak Airo, will welcome their first customers tomorrow on the Cascades route. To celebrate the launch, Amtrak invited Seattle Transit Blog and other media organizations to tour and ride one of the new trains this past Saturday. The event kicked off with a marching band and speeches from leaders at Amtrak, the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA), Washington State, and Siemens Mobility. After the event in Seattle, the train traveled south to Portland for another event before ending the day in Eugene.

Amtrak Airo trainsets consist of one locomotive, one Business Class car, one cafe car, and four Coach Class cars. The last Coach car also has a luggage compartment and operator cab. Compared to the current Amtrak Cascades rolling stock, these trains will provide a more reliable and comfortable trip for up to 317 passengers. While Amtrak Cascades has a 79mph speed limit for most of its route, Airo trains will reach their top speed of 125mph when they run on the Northeast Corridor staring next year.

Passengers can expect modern amenities throughout the train. Several information screens are located in every car to share details about the next stop, restroom location, and other announcements. Between each car, the vestibules are fully enclosed to prevent rain or snow from entering the train. Each passenger car has large windows next to every row and a manual shade for sunny trips.

Business Class seats are located in the first car and have a 2-1 configuration. The Airo trainsets have 47 Business Class seats and 3 handicap spaces. Seat assignments are supported so Businesses Class travelers can guarantee seats next to their travel companions. There are three 4-seat tables, two 2-seat tables, and two adjustable table handicap spaces.

The seats not at a table each have a small tray table, large tray table, device holder, drink holder, coat hanger, and footrest. All seats in Business Class feature an adjustable headrest, reading light, 2 full outlets, and several USB-C charging ports.

All seats on the Airo trainsets use the bottom out recline technique. Rather than pushing the seat back into the next row, the seats recline by sliding the bottom of the seat forward to adjust the angle of the seat back.
Cars 3, 4, 5, and 6 offer seats in Coach Class positioned in a 2-2 configuration. Despite name screens located above every seat, Amtrak Cascades does not support seat reservations in Coach Class.
While narrower, each seat has a similar tray table configuration to a Business Class seat. Each pair of seats has 2 full outlets and 2 USB-C charging ports.

Each Amtrak Airo trainset has several restrooms located throughout the train. All restrooms are fully accessible and feature a mechanical sliding door (opened/closed with a button), touchless faucets, changing table, mirror light, and a small shelf for a purse or other personal items.

Amtrak has implemented a number of upgrades for passengers using mobility devices. Tables used by passengers in handicap spaces have an adjustable height. This allows passengers to have a comfortable experience regardless of the size of their wheelchair or mobility aid. In addition, ceiling reading lights have been added above handicap spaces to provide a similar utility as the lights mounted to every seat.

The cafe car has been redesigned on the Airo trainsets. The cafe offers a selection meals, snacks, and drinks. On Amtrak Cascades, passengers can still enjoy Ivar’s Clam Chowder and sandwiches from Alki Bakery. The cafe car has a water bottle refill station and a few rows of seats for passengers to use while dining.

Amtrak Airo offers a significant increase in bike storage over the older trains on Amtrak Cascades. Each Airo trainset has capacity for 18 bikes. Bike racks are located throughout the train and in the luggage compartment. In Coach Class cars, some luggage racks can be folded down for bike storage when needed. While bikes of all shapes and sizes are gaining popularity in the PNW, only bikes that meet Amtrak’s nationwide guidelines are permitted onboard. These guidelines include a 50lb maximum weight and 2in max tire width. E-bikes are permitted as carry-on items.
Note: Amtrak is still updating its bike reservation system to account for the increased bike capacity on Amtrak Airo. As a result, reservations may still be limited to 6 bikes per train.

Starting tomorrow, Amtrak Airo trains will be used trips between Seattle and Eugene on trains 503 and 508 and between Seattle and Vancouver, BC on trains 516 and 519. A third Airo train is ready for service and will be kept in Seattle as a spare. During the first few weeks of operations, additional Amtrak staff will be onboard each trip to assist passengers and handle any minor technical issues.

Five more Airo trainsets will be arriving in Seattle over the next few months. Each train will need to undergo further testing and validation on the Cascades corridor before entering service. Amtrak expects all Airo trains to be in service on the Cascades route by next summer.

articles.title: Pending Fiscal Cliff at SDOT Prompts Major Budget Shifts
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) is making "dynamic changes" to its budget for the rest of 2026 all the way through 2028 to sidestep a major looming budget shortfall. Those adjustments are set to cause some painful cuts, and significantly limit the ability of Mayor Katie Wilson's administration to prioritize new transportation projects in the future.
Across the next two years, SDOT's budget is set to take a 4% hit that will impact nearly half of the department's programs, in the hopes of getting things back on a more sustainable path.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in the home stretch! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us exceed our goal!

The financial issues creeping up on SDOT are impacting the transportation fund, the primary source of transportation funding outside of the $1.55 billion, eight-year transportation levy voters approved in 2024 . According to a presentation made to the Seattle City Council's budget committee Monday, SDOT would have been looking at a $113 million deficit in the transportation fund by 2028 without any adjustments.

"Our costs have continued to rise while revenues have flattened or declined, resulting in recent budget appropriations outpacing available resources and driving down our fund balances," Kris Castleman, SDOT's Director of Finance & Administration, told councilmembers Monday. "We are at a critical financial inflection point, and targeted intervention is needed now to balance the budget, maintain cash to fund our daily operations, and safeguard our future with a path toward long-term financial stability."

These adjustments to SDOT's budget come as part of Mayor Katie Wilson's $9.1 billion draft budget , unveiled last week. The new mayor's first budget, the package has drawn attention for being more focused on setting the city on a sustainable path , putting the days of continued projected deficits in out years behind it after heavy usage under former Mayor Bruce Harrell.

Changes to SDOT's budget already made in 2026 include $56.7 million in reductions, including nearly $14 million in program cuts. Milder winter weather earlier this year allowed the department's emergency services budget to be cut by 56%, and planned maintenance work on the city's traffic signals were moved to 2027, resulting in a 39% cut in that program. But reductions in future years will be more painful, and include cuts to pothole repair and major bridge maintenance projects.

With a reduction in pothole repair funding, SDOT expects to slip closer to its voter-approved target of filling 80% of reported potholes within 72 hours, compared to its nearly 90% rate reported currently. Major repaving work on city arterial streets will rebound to historic levels, despite a boost in maintenance funding from the Seattle Transportation Levy put forward by Harrell and expanded by Council.

2026 adjustments have also included the "abandonment" of years of capital funds that had been carried forward from prior years but didn't get utilized. The practice of carrying funds forward from the prior year after the department wasn't able to spend all of its budget has been one that has been ongoing for years, and has often made it hard to truly understand the department's financial outlook.

The proposed cuts will have some staffing impacts. Out of 1,291 total full-time positions at SDOT, nine positions that are currently unfilled will be permanently eliminated, including three civic engineer positions, three signal electricians, two maintenance laborers, and one traffic sign and signal crew chief. But the department's staff capacity will be largely insulated from cuts – at least for now.

Also insulated from cuts are traffic safety programs, with Acting SDOT Director Angela Brady telling councilmembers that the Vision Zero budget for 2026-2028 is actually set to increase by $1 million across the three years. However, many more projects than just the ones in the Vision Zero program impact safety, and even reductions in the pothole program can impact safety for people who walk and roll on Seattle's streets.

"I want to be clear that street safety and Vision Zero, as a program, remain fully funded in this budget," Brady said. "We know how important this program is to Seattle citizens, our mayor, and our councilmembers."

Wilson, in her budget speech last week , also called out transit speed and reliability investments as an area where focus will be maintained, in the wake of the successful implementation of a long-envisioned bus lane on Denny Way for the Route 8. That $5 million project was funded by the 2024 transportation levy.
Additional funds for bus upgrades are included in Wilson's renewal of the Seattle Transit Measure, on the ballot in November.
While more streets are being eyed for bus lanes, those projects aren't moving forward with the alacrity of the mayoral-directed Denny Way project.
Such a dramatic adjustment to scale back programs will absolutely have an impact on the ability for Wilson – and for city councilmembers – to get new projects added to SDOT's workplan.

"We also want to note that today's updates about reductions, limited reserves, and uncertain funding make our overall position to handle new requests less flexible," Castleman said. "New priorities, projects, programs, and policies that are unfunded can present a zero-sum game in this financial environment. So, as we engage with communities, businesses and our elected leadership, folks are likely to hear even more from SDOT about trade-offs."
During Monday's meeting, a question from Councilmember Dionne Foster probed into the issues with the transportation fund, and how this issue has popped up seemingly out of nowhere.

"With the transportation fund, this has been building for several years," City Budget Director Aly Pennucci said. "As a city, we have been hyperfocused on the general fund deficit, and there's been less public conversation about the projected deficit in the transportation fund that was not ideal, but was present in the financial plan that was part of the adopted budget last year, and then the combination of actual expenses, actual revenues, and the automatic carry forward in the capital budget kind of all came to a head."

Wilson's proposed budget for SDOT does pull a few levers in hopes of improving the department's financial picture. It increases the city's Commercial Parking Tax rate from 14.5% to 17%, a move that brings in nearly $10 million per year that will go to both Vision Zero and programs like sign maintenance and urban forestry that would otherwise see steeper cuts.

Traffic enforcement cameras are also expected to be a budget lifeline, with an additional $20 million per year by 2028 expected following the expansion of the speed camera program beyond time-limited school zones next year. Pennucci told councilmembers that those projections are conservative, given the fact that SDOT has not yet implemented 24/7 speed cameras on any arterial corridors.

A new 0.1% countywide sales tax for county roads will also benefit SDOT, thanks to a forthcoming pass-through program intended to fund local transportation needs. In June, when the creation of that program was being debated, it nearly included a provision that would have capped Seattle's contributions as the largest city in the county, but that cap was removed after pushing by city leaders and advocates. As a result, $4.7 million a year is set to prevent cuts to SDOT's urban forestry program and some bridge maintenance work.

At Monday's initial discussion of SDOT's budget, councilmembers raised concerns around projects in their districts potentially getting shortchanged, including a lack of ongoing funding for the council-created District Project Fund . A proposal that was spearheaded by transportation chair Rob Saka, that fund provided $7 million in 2025 and 2026 for hand-picked transportation projects in each of the seven council districts, but no ongoing funding for that fund had been identified beyond this year. If the District Project Fund is to continue, it will fall on the council to decide what other line items should be cut from the department's budget.
The hope is that by overhauling SDOT's budget and "right-sizing" program budgets to align with available resources, the department can be put on more stable footing.

"What is especially urgent for us is that our flexible funding sources are becoming even more tightly constrained, and yet they are used for core services and help us to be responsive to emerging needs from both our elected officials and the community," Castleman said. "We're also addressing the very real need to create financial stability for the department."
The Seattle City Council will hold a public hearing on Wilson's draft budget next Tuesday, October 5 , at 1 pm and 5 pm.

articles.author: Wesley Lin
paras: On September 18, Sound Transit released the Environmental impact Statement for the Everett Link extension . This light rail extension will extend the Link light rail system north towards Everett from Lynnwood. The first phase plans to build the West Alderwood , Ash Way , Mariner , and finally the SW Everett Industrial Center by 2037. The second phase would extend it north to Everett with SR 526/Evergreen and Everett Station by 2041. There is also one unfunded provisional station at SR 99/Airport Road .
The draft EIS comment period is open until November 2nd.

This article will mostly focus on the first phase up to SW Everett Industrial Center. Most of the station alignments were previously discussed in The Urbanist as well. This discussion will focus on the details of the preferred options. Unless otherwise cited, all images are from the Sound Transit online open house .
From Lynnwood station, the line would continue north along the west side of I-5 then turn east near 33rd Ave W.

Among the alternatives considered, the preferred alternative is ALD-2D (Northern Mall Alignment with 33rd Avenue Station) shown in green. The first stop is West Alderwood next to Alderwood Mall. High retail activity and surrounding apartments should drive strong ridership.
The ALD-2D option will place the elevated station to the west of Alderwood Mall next to the JC Penney.
For the preferred alternative of ALD-D the three bus routes of 121, 122, and Swift orange would stop there. For the other alternatives of ALD-B and ALD-F the Swift Orange bus might skip the station.

There are some alternative options moving the station to the north or south of Alderwood Mall instead. Most of them have moderate tradeoffs with which properties would need to displaced. All of them would cost approximately the same at $1 billion.

From Alderwood Mall, the line would the continue north along I-5. There is no preferred alternative for this segment. The Ash Way station would be near the 164th St SW and I-5 intersection. The Swift Orange BRT would help connect residents along 164th St SW to the station. The line would reuse the existing Ash Way Park-and-Ride for parking.
ASH-1A (West of I-5 Alignment with Ash Way Park-and-Ride Station) has the line staying west of I-5. This would build the elevated Ash Way station next to the Ash Way Park-and-Ride.

The other option ASH-2D (East of I-5 Alignment with 164th Street Station) would build it on the east of I-5. One complication is that this would be complicated for the station to connect to the existing west transit facilities.
Snohomish County explored fixing the east station issues with the I-5/164th St SW Direct Access Improvements project to build an HOV/pedestrian bridge just north of 164th Street.
Assuming the I-5 overpass is built, the routes 112, 121, m103, 117, n14 and m2 will terminate at Ash Way. Swift Orange line will also using the crossing and continue along it.

The option ASH-1A staying on the west of I-5 supposedly costs more than ASH-2D. However, I’m somewhat skeptical of the numbers considering ASH-2D requires an expensive bridge across I-5 while ASH-1A stays on the same side.
After Ash Way, the line will continue north along I-5 to the Mariner Station. Clusters of garden-style apartments along 128th St SW will generate strong residential ridership.
The MAR-1B (South of 128th Street Alignment with 8th Avenue Station) alternative will build the elevated Mariner station just south of 128th St SW.
The Mariner station would serve as the transfer point for many bus routes around South Everett.
The Swift Orange will likely be extended one mile and terminate at Mariner Station instead of its current terminus at McCollum P&R.

Once the line reaches Mariner, the train will then head west along Airport Road. There is the provisional unfunded SR 99 / Airport Road station at the intersection. This SR 99 / Airport Road is surrounded by mostly light industrial and commercial properties however it would also be a pretty vital half-way point transfer point for the Swift Blue BRT line.

The SW Everett Industrial Center station (a somewhat laborious way to say Boeing) will be built near Paine Field and the Everett Boeing factory. There has been some competing priorities of whether to build this station on the north nearby Boeing for the workers or whether to build it to the west near Paine Field for passengers.
The SWI-1A (Airport Road/SR 526 Alignment with SR 526 Station) is the preferred Alternative. This would place it closest to the Seaway Transit center that Boeing workers currently use.
One complication is that most of the buses would have to take a circuitous route to reach the Seaway Transit Center. A pedestrian bridge might be built to connect the station to Boeing across SR 526.

The SWI-1B alternative places it in the mid point between the airport and Boeing. While the SWI-1C alternative places the station closest to the airport. Also interestingly, there would be an airport shuttle bus with all three station sites from the station to Paine Field airport.
These next two stations will be built in a later phase by 2041.
After SW Everett Industrial Center, the line will continue east along SR 526 to SR 526/Evergreen station. There are five alternatives here with much community pushback. We’ll go over EGN-A and EGN-E.

The EGN-A alternative will place it just north of the SR 526 freeway with the least property impacts. This places it closer to apartments such as the Four Corners and the Cascade High School. A pedestrian bridge will be built to make it easier to cross south of the freeway. However, it is also tricky to transfer to some buses.
The EGN-E places it just south of W Casino Road.
Both alternatives would connect to the Swift Blue and the future Swift Silver Line (labeled as a rerouted Green Line above).
One advantage of the EGN-E station closer to Casino Ave, is that it is easier for a bus to reach Everett Mall.
The main preferred alternative is EVT-1A (Smith Avenue Alignment) which places the Everett light rail station closest to the existing Sounder Everett station.
EVT-A would be an elevated station at the corner of Smith Ave and 32nd St.

Sound Transit has not yet decided where to place the new Operations and Maintenance Facility (OMF). One of the above three spots will be picked. The OMF is used for train maintenance, cleaning, and storage.

The projected ridership with the initial phase (in green) and second phase (in pink) is shown above. The highest daily ridership is projected at Everett Station with 10,700 riders. The next two highest are Ash Way and Mariner with approximately 4,600 riders. Mariner would have an estimated 7,000 riders (2,400 more) with the initial phase due to I-5 freeway buses from Everett truncating there.

The Everett Link extension will mostly benefit trips within the Everett and North Lynnwood area and not improve the freeway trips between Everett and destinations south of Lynnwood. Sound Transit estimates 29 minutes from Lynnwood station to Everett station which is on par with the current freeway bus times.

The original operating plan for the ST3 calls for the 3 Line to serve all stations between Lynnwood and Everett. In addition, the 2 Line will be extended to Mariner station. During peak hours, Sound Transit plans to provide 3 minute frequency for the West Alderwood, Ash Way, and Mariner stations. North of Mariner, frequency will drop to 6 minutes.

With the phased implementation plan, the exact operation plan is not clear. In addition, the exact lines that serve the new stations will also depend on the opening timelines for other ST3 extensions to West Seattle and Ballard.

articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: 2026 has been a big year for trains in Puget Sound. In January, the Federal Way Link Extension completed its first full month of operation. Simulated service on the 2 Line began in February , providing 4 minute frequencies for the first time between Seattle and Lynnwood. In March, the Crosslake Connection finally connected the 2 Line with Seattle. Link ridership jumped 46% in April thanks to the new service across Lake Washington. In May, the Sound Transit Board confirmed funding for several ST3 Link extensions (at the cost of other extensions). In June, Sound Transit welcomed passengers aboard new Sounder trains and set multiple Link ridership records . The USA vs Belgium World Cup match in early July helped Link surpass 300,000 passengers in one day for the first time ever. Last month, transit agencies in Snohomish, King, and Pierce counties restructured their bus networks to cement Link as the backbone for regional transportation in Puget Sound.
To add to the list, Sound Transit is opening a new Link station and Amtrak is rolling out next-generation trains in September.

On September 30, Amtrak Cascades will welcome the first passengers aboard new Amtrak Airo trainsets. Amtrak Airo are trains built by Siemens that will soon run on many short distance Amtrak routes across the country. The first three of eight trains for the Cascades route are in Seattle and will operate on two roundtrips daily. The remaining five trainsets will enter service as they complete testing. An additional 75 Amtrak Airo trainsets will begin serving other routes around the country next year.

While the new trains will not reduce travel times or offer more daily trips, these trains can carry more passengers (over 300 seats per train), will be more reliable, and are more comfortable than the aging rolling stock currently used on Amtrak Cascades. Passengers can expect adjustable headrests, panoramic windows, enhanced lighting, and modern interiors.
Beginning September 30, Amtrak Airo trains will be used on the following Amtrak Cascades trips.
Between Seattle and Eugene: Train 503: Seattle to Eugene at 7:10am – 1:48pm Train 508: Eugene to Seattle at 4:30pm – 10:50pm
Between Seattle and Vancouver: Train 516: Seattle to Vancouver, B.C. at 8:30am – 12:30pm Train 519: Vancouver, B.C. to Seattle at 4:45pm – 9:10pm

Seattle Transit Blog will share a first look at the Amtrak Airo trains on Tuesday, including pictures and videos from a trip on the train. Until then, check out this Bluesky thread with highlights from the media tour on Saturday.

Also on September 30, Sound Transit will begin service at Pinehurst station. Pinehurst station is the agency’s first Link in-fill station and is located between Northgate and Shoreline South/148th stations. This the second piece of the ST3 measure to be completed (after Downtown Redmond Link) and will be the last Link station to open until Graham Street station in 2031. Pinehurst station is served by the new Metro Route 77 which connects the station with Bitter Lake and Lake City. 1 Line and 2 Line trains will begin stopping at Pinehurst station at 5am on September 30. The very first train to serve Pinehurst is a 2 Line train that departs Wilburton at 4:04am and arrives at Pinehurst at 5:05am.

To celebrate the new station, Sound Transit is hosting an event from 2pm-6pm on Wednesday. The event will include live music, local organizations, sponsors, food, an interactive activity with station artist Romson Bustillo, and the ST Shop merchandise booth.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Seattle’s University District
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. So, here’s a short list to get you started.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: The 38 Best Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. Every place on the list has been open for at least six months, proving its merit.

Like many menus, this map updates every quarter — removal from the Eater 38 doesn’t mean a restaurant isn’t still awesome and won’t return in the future. New to the map as of August 2026: unassuming neighborhood gem Three Sacks Full; seafood-focused French bistro L’Oursin; and La Cabaña, where you can find some of the city’s best pupusas.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
